Improved Lower Bounds for QAC0
Malvika Raj Joshi

Abstract
In this work, we establish the strongest known lower bounds against QAC0, while allowing its full power of polynomially many ancillae and gates. Our two main results show that:
1.
Depth 3 QAC0 circuits cannot compute PARITY regardless of size, and require at least \Omega(\exp(\sqrt{n})) many gates to compute MAJORITY.
2.
Depth 2 circuits cannot approximate high-influence Boolean functions (e.g., PARITY) with non-negligible advantage, regardless of size.
We present new techniques for simulating certain QAC0 circuits classically in AC0 to obtain our depth 3 lower bounds. In these results, we relax the output requirement of the quantum circuit to a single bit (i.e., no restrictions on input preservation/reversible computation), making our depth 2 approximation bound stronger than the previous best bound of [24]. This also enables us to draw natural comparisons with classical AC0 circuits, which can compute PARITY exactly in depth 2 using exponential size. Our proof techniques further suggest that, for boolean total functions, QAC0 circuits do not necessarily provide more power than their classical counterparts. Our third result shows that depth 2 QAC0 circuits, regardless of size, cannot exactly synthesize an n-target nekomata state (a state whose synthesis is directly related to the computation of PARITY). This complements the depth 2 exponential size upper bound of [24] for approximating nekomata (which is used as a sub-circuit in the only known constant depth PARITY upper bound).
Finally, we argue that approximating PARITY in QAC0, with at least 1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n) advantage on average, is just as hard as computing it exactly. Thus, extending our techniques to higher depths would also rule out approximate circuits for PARITY and related problems.

A Approximate to Exact PARITY Deferred Proofs
1 Introduction
In classical computation, the ability to copy information is considered an elementary operation. Every major classically studied circuit class—e.g. NC, AC, and TC—trivially contains the FAN-OUT operation. Quantumly, however, the ability to copy information is more limited and nuanced. For example, the no-cloning theorem explicitly prohibits copying quantum information. Interestingly, even the ability to copy classical information, via the quantum FAN-OUT gate, appears to offer substantial power in the quantum setting.
The relative power of the FAN-OUT operation in the classical and quantum settings has largely been formalized through the study of three circuit classes: AC0, QAC0, and QAC{}^{0}_{f}. AC0 is the class of polynomial-sized, constant-depth circuits comprised of unlimited fan-in  and  and OR operations, with NOT s allowed on the inputs and arbitrary FAN-OUT.
Following the seminal works of [10, 1, 30], the celebrated work of [15] introduced the switching lemma, which proved tight exponential lower bounds on the size of bounded-depth AC0 circuits computing or even approximating PARITY. Later, [18] used this technique to establish low-degree Fourier concentration of Boolean functions implementable by AC0. Beyond profound implications for fields such as cryptography and learning theory, these results demonstrated that high-degree functions cannot be approximated by AC0.
Subsequent works refined this picture: [27] proved essentially tight bounds on the Fourier spectrum of AC0, while [16] established an average-case depth hierarchy theorem, showing that increased depth strictly increases the power of AC0 even on random inputs.
In 1999, Moore proposed the QAC0 circuit class as a natural quantum analog of AC0 [19] (later published in the work of [11]). QAC0 (QAC{}^{0}_{f}, resp.) is the class of polynomial-sized, constant-depth quantum circuits comprised of arbitrary single-qubit gates and generalized Toffoli gates (with unbounded FAN-OUT gates, resp.). Moore also posed the following fundamental question:
Is FAN-OUT \in QAC0? Equivalently, is QAC0 = QAC{}^{0}_{f}?
Note that, quantumly, FAN-OUT is equivalent to PARITY, up to Hadamard conjugation [19]. Therefore, this question can equivalently be framed as:
Is PARITY \in QAC0?
Resolving this question would have several profound implications for quantum complexity and quantum computation. In the classical AC0 setting, even allowing PARITY (i.e., \texttt{MOD}_{2}) gates does not yield \texttt{MOD}_{m} for general m [23, 25]. In sharp contrast, if FAN-OUT/PARITY \in QAC0, then:
1.
QAC0 contains FAN-OUT, and thus AC0 and is substantially more powerful than AC0 [19] (PARITY \notin AC0  [15]).
2.
For any integer m, \texttt{MOD}_{m} can be implemented in QAC0 [11].
3.
n-qubit GHZ (cat) states can be prepared in constant depth using only single-qubit gates and a single \texttt{FAN-OUT}/\texttt{PARITY} operation [19, 17].
4.
QAC0 can perform many powerful computations, including: majority, threshold[t], exact[t], counting, sorting, arithmetic, phase estimation, and the quantum Fourier transform [17].
5.
Strong pseudo-random unitaries (PRUs) are implementable in QAC0 [9].
6.
The quantum shallow-depth hierarchy collapses, i.e. QNC{}^{0}_{f} = QAC{}^{0}_{f} =QTC{}^{0}_{f} and these classes can be characterized by just FAN-OUT gates and single qubit unitaries [26].
Furthermore, since QAC0 includes gates of unbounded width, standard light-cone techniques are insufficient for proving circuit lower-bounds. Thus, resolving whether PARITY \in QAC0 will likely result in novel techniques for proving more general quantum circuit lower-bounds. In fact, previously-developed techniques have already led to exciting applications. For example, QAC0 Fourier concentration established by the lower-bound approach of [20] led to sample-efficient algorithms for learning single-output QAC0 channels [20, 3] and a time-efficient algorithm for average-case learning of QAC0 unitaries [28]. Additionally, the exponential-size implementation of PARITY in QAC0 proposed by [24] enabled the compression of strong QAC{}^{0}_{f} PRUs to weak QAC0 PRUs by [9].
Despite substantial effort in proving both upper and lower-bounds [7, 22, 24, 20, 2, 8], Moore’s question has remained unresolved for nearly three decades. Prior to this work, the strongest known PARITY lower-bounds were
either in the setting with limited, slightly super-linear, ancillae [2] or with unlimited ancillae, but only up to depth-2 [24, 8].
As demonstrated by the only known constant-depth upper-bound for PARITY [24], and lower-bounds against circuits with limited ancillae [20, 2], the main power of QAC0 circuits comes from their use of super-linear ancillae to generate entanglement, accounting for the lack of FAN-OUT.
In this work, we introduce novel techniques for proving QAC0 circuit lower-bounds, enabling us to give the strongest fixed-depth lower-bounds for QAC0 to-date, while still allowing its full power of polynomial ancillae. In Section 4, we prove the first depth-3 lower-bounds for QAC0, ruling out computation of exact PARITY and MAJORITY with sub-exponential size. For PARITY specifically, we further prove a size-independent depth-3 lower-bound.
In Section 5, we also prove a Fourier-tail decay bound for depth-2 QAC0 circuits with unlimited ancillae, demonstrating that they have low total influence. For these results, we treat the output of the circuit as a single bit on a designated register with no constraints on other registers. This makes our depth-2 lower bounds stronger than the previously known
depth-2 approximation bound of [24] which requires the circuit to preserve the state on the input registers. This also allows us to draw analogies with classical AC0, where the output is a single bit. Interestingly, our results contrast what is known for classical circuits, since exponential-size AC0 circuits can compute PARITY exactly in depth-2.
Finally, in Section 6, we show that depth-2 QAC0 circuits cannot exactly synthesize a so-called “nekomata” state, which is closely related to FAN-OUT. For example, [24] achieves a constant-depth upper-bound for PARITY by first using an exponential-size depth-2 QAC circuit to approximately synthesize a nekomata state. We show that such a state on n=\omega(1) targets cannot be exactly prepared in depth-2, even with unlimited ancillae. This complements the only known O(1)-depth upper-bound for approximating nekomatas, due to [24].
We present new techniques for simulating QAC0 circuits for exact computation of boolean functions in AC0. Although it is known that QAC0 (or even QNC0) provides more power than AC0 for search problems [29], and worst-case bounded error regimes for decision problems (BQAC0) [12], there are no known decision separations in which QAC0 circuit is exact.
We justify our approach in Appendix A though a QAC0 reduction from exactly computing PARITY to approximating PARITY with any inverse-polylogarithmic advantage on a random input. We conclude that it is sufficient to establish lower bounds against exact QAC0 circuits for any of the problems connected to PARITY described above [11, 17, 13], to also rule out these approximate regimes.

We will now briefly summarize known QAC0 upper-bounds, lower-bounds, and structural results prior to this work, as listed in Table 1. We will first discuss QAC0 lower-bounds for PARITY, which can be split into two main categories: (i) restricted-ancillae and (ii) restricted-depth. We will also describe corresponding QAC0 low-degree structural results and nekomata/CAT state preparation lower-bounds. Finally, we conclude by describing the only known upper-bound for approximately computing PARITY and nekomata states in QAC0, using exponential ancillae.
Restricted-Ancillae PARITY Lower-Bounds.
The size of a QAC0 circuit is closely related to the number of ancillae it uses.
By definition, the number of ancillae in QAC0 circuits is allowed to be an arbitrary polynomial in n.
The first category of PARITY lower-bounds [7, 5, 20, 2] focuses on generic depth-d QAC0 circuits with ancillae limited to o(n^{2}).
The proofs of [20, 2] follow by showing that the circuit’s Heisenberg-evolved single-qubit “output” measurement Pauli/projector can be approximated, to high precision, by low-degree objects. Beyond ruling out the computation of PARITY, these low-degree structural results enable correlation bounds against generic high-degree Boolean functions, such as MAJORITY and \texttt{MOD}_{k}. The key caveat of this low-degree approach, however, is that it only holds for a depth dependent number of ancillae, which [2] pushed to slightly super-linear in n for arbitrary constant-depth QAC0 circuits.
Restricted-Depth PARITY Lower-Bounds.
The second category of PARITY lower-bounds focuses on fixed-depth QAC circuits, without any extra constraints on the ancillae. Specifically, [24] established a depth-2 average-case approximate lower-bound, while [8] established a depth-2 worst-case exact lower-bound against PARITY \in QAC0 , both with unlimited ancillae. All the known lower bounds that do not impose any restrictions on the number of ancillae beyond the default \text{poly}(n) fall under this category and only go up to depth-2. Both the upper and lower bounds of [24] correspond to circuits with an n-bit output that preserve the state on the input qubits, and we refer to these circuits as “input-preserving”.
CAT/Nekomata Lower-Bounds.
In [19], Moore proved that there exist reductions between computing PARITY/FAN-OUT and preparing the n-qubit CAT state, \ket{\hbox{\hbox to8.18pt{\vbox to8.43pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.08804pt\lower-3.20981pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.40042pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}{{}}{}{{{}}

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}_{n}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\ket{0^{n}}+\ket{1^{n}}\right). In recent work [24], Rosenthal introduced the notion of an n-qubit “nekomata” state, of form
\displaystyle\ket{\text{Nekomata}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\ket{0^{n}}\ket{\psi_{\alpha}}+\ket{1^{n}}\ket{\psi_{\beta}}\right).
(1)
The nekomata is similar to \ket{{}_{n}}, but allows for each branch to have an arbitrary ancillary state (i.e. the normalized states \ket{\psi_{\alpha}} and \ket{\psi_{\beta}}). In this case, where the two branches are equally weighted (with probability 1/2), we refer to the state as a “balanced” nekomata.
[24] showed O(1)-depth reductions between preparing n-qubit nekomata states and computing FAN-OUT/PARITY, analogous to those for \ket{{}_{n}}, and extended all these reductions to the approximate setting. Rosenthal also showed that any depth-d QAC0 circuit that approximates an n-qubit nekomata must have \Omega(n/(d+1)) multi-qubit gates acting on the targets.
PARITY and Nekomata Upper-Bounds.
Despite several lower-bound results for QAC0, there is only one known upper-bound for approximating PARITY in constant-depth QAC.
Notably, [24] gave a depth-7 QAC circuit for approximating n-qubit PARITY, using \exp(n^{1-o(1)}) gates (thereby requiring more resources than permitted in polynomial-sized QAC0). To achieve this, Rosenthal first gave a depth-2 circuit using an approximate n-qubit nekomata and then used it to obtain a depth-7 circuit for approximating PARITY. Due to the recursive nature of PARITY, for any depth k=7d, this implies QAC0 circuits of size roughly \exp(n^{1/d}) approximating PARITY.
1.2 Our Results
In this work we study fixed-depth QAC circuits, specifically with depth-\leq 3, and do not impose additional restrictions on ancillae. Note that for constant depth circuits, limiting the ancillae also limits the size of the circuit because each qubit can belong to at most d gates. Our motivation for studying fixed-depth QAC circuits stems from the large gap between the only known constant-depth upper-bound for PARITY [24], which uses an exponential number of gates, and
the best known techniques for arbitrary-depth circuits [7, 20, 2], which fail to rule out even O(n^{2})-sized circuits for depth-\geq 2.
Our main results are summarized below.
Our first result shows that depth-3 circuits (i) cannot compute MAJORITY using only sub-exponential gates and (ii) cannot compute PARITY regardless of size. The informal theorem statement is as follows, with the full proof given in Section 4 (Theorem 4.7). We note that both results apply regardless of the number of ancillae.
Theorem 1.1 (Depth-3 MAJORITY Lower-bound).
Let C be a depth-3 QAC0 circuit C on n inputs with m\leq 2^{n^{o(1)}} gates such that on every input \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, C produces the state \ket{f(\bm{x})}_{t} on a designated output t. Then, f(\bm{x}) cannot be the PARITY or MAJORITY function.
Theorem 1.2 (Depth-3 PARITY Size-Independent Bound).
Let C be a depth-3 QAC0 circuit with n>100 input qubits and an arbitrary number of ancillae and gates, such that on every input \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the circuit C produces the state \ket{f(\bm{x})}_{t} on a designated output qubit t. Then, f cannot be the PARITY function.
We prove these depth-3 lower-bounds in Section 4, by first showing that, after applying a quantum restriction (that keeps \Omega(n) input bits alive),
the output of the remaining depth-(\leq 3) QAC0 circuit can be simulated by a classical AC0 circuit of a slightly larger depth and size (Section 2.3.3). This immediately implies an \exp(n^{\Omega(1)})-size lower-bound due to known lower-bounds for PARITY in AC0 [15]. Our techniques also apply to other functions that behave MAJORITY giving us the first lower-bound against the MAJORITY function for QAC0 circuits with polynomial ancillae.
We observe that at very low depths (\leq 2), QAC0 circuits exhibit certain monotonicity properties. For PARITY we can exploit these properties to strengthen the bound from Theorem 1.1 to a size-independent bound, Theorem 1.2, using carefully-designed classical restrictions. These restrictions rely on the property of the PARITY function being invariant under arbitrary classical restrictions, unlike MAJORITY, which requires balanced restrictions. Moreover, PARITY and MAJORITY are known to be equivalent up to a O(1) factor in depth for QAC circuits [17]. Thus we expect PARITY lower bounds for higher depths to depend on the size as in Theorem 1.1.
Our second main result is a structural result for depth-2 QAC0 circuits. Namely, we show these circuits have low total influence, regardless of the number of ancillae. The informal theorem statement is as follows, with the full proof given in Section 5 (Theorem 5.1).
Theorem 1.3 (Depth-2 Influence Upper-Bound).
Let C be a depth-2 QAC0 circuit with n input qubits and of ancillae.
Consider the function f_{C}:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to[0,1] defined by f_{C}(x)=\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\text{$C$ accepts $x$}]. Then, f_{C} has total influence O(\log n).
First, note that this result is tight. Specifically, consider the Tribes function \texttt{TRIBES}(x)=\lor_{i=1}^{s}\land_{j=1}^{w}x_{i,j} that can be exactly implemented by depth-2 QAC0 circuits with s+1 ancillae and has {\mathbf{Inf}}[f]=\Theta(\log n) for a specific choice of parameters (s=\Theta(n/\log n) and w=\Theta(\log n)).
Theorem 1.3 follows from a proof of stronger Fourier tail bounds for functions computable by depth-2 QAC0 circuits, using novel entropy-based arguments. We also use these improved Fourier tail bounds to prove the following correlation bound against PARITY (see Corollary 5.9), thus ruling out the approximate computation of PARITY in depth-2 QAC0.
Corollary 1.4.
f_{C} has correlation at most \exp(-\Omega(\sqrt{n})) with PARITY.
Our next result is a depth-2 unlimited ancillae QAC0 lower-bound against exact preparation of nekomata states. In fact, we are able to rule out a depth-2 circuit for creating any entangled state that only has nonzero amplitude in two subspaces, corresponding to the all 0s, \ket{{\vec{0}}}_{[n]} and all 1s, \ket{{\vec{1}}}_{[n]} branches on any set of n>1 “target” qubits. We call such states, as below, “generalized nekomatas”,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi}=\alpha\ket{0^{n}}\ket{\psi_{\alpha}}+\beta\ket{1^{n}}\ket{\psi_{\beta}},
\displaystyle\qquad\text{with }\alpha\neq 0\text{ and }\beta\neq 0.
(2)
The informal theorem statement is as follows, with the full proof given in Section 6 (Corollary 6.1).
Theorem 1.5 (Depth-2 Nekomata Lower-Bound).
A depth-2 QAC0 circuit with an arbitrary number of ancillae and gates cannot exactly prepare a “generalized” nekomata on n>4 targets.
Note that this bound is also tight, since any \ket{{}_{n}} is also a n-nekomata and we can construct the state \ket{{}_{4}} in depth-2 by constructing \ket{{}_{2}}=\ket{\mathrm{EPR}} in depth-1. Rosenthal [24] gave a circuit for approximating an n-nekomata with exponential ancillae in depth-2, which is then used as a sub-circuit to obtain a parity circuit. Our result implies that such an approximation cannot be made exact by simply using more ancillae, thus ruling out the exact analog of Rosenthal’s parity circuit in the same depth.
Note that we define these generalized nekomata states only to aid proving our depth-2 bound against balanced nekomatas and we do not expect highly unbalanced instances to be useful or powerful. For example, the state \sqrt{(1-\varepsilon)}\cdot\ket{0^{n}}+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\cdot\ket{1^{n}}, which is a generalized n-nekomata, can be simply approximated by \ket{0^{n}}.
Our final result provides evidence for the robustness of our exact lower-bound techniques by showing that computing PARITY approximately on a random input in QAC0 is just as hard as computing it exactly.
The informal statement is as below,
Theorem 1.6 (1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)-adv for PARITY is equivalent to exact in QAC0).
Let C be a depth-d QAC0 circuit with n input qubits and a ancillae such that f_{C}(\bm{x}), the acceptance probability of C has correlation at least 1/\log(n)^{\delta} with PARITY. Then, there exists a depth-O(d) with circuit with O(a\cdot n^{\delta}) ancillae that exactly computes PARITY on n qubits.
We describe the main ideas behind this reduction in Section 2.6 (Theorem 2.2). The formal proof follows though a combination of several standard QAC0 techniques and we include it in appendix A.
2 Techniques
2.1 Key Challenges and High-Level Intuition
The main challenge in proving lower-bounds for QAC0 circuits stems from their ability to use multiple ancilla qubits in a single gate. In contrast, the concept of ancillae is foreign to classical AC0 circuits, as they have no advantage in using ancillae (e.g., they can be replaced with FAN-OUT).
Perhaps a more suitable classical analogue of the use of ancillae in QAC0 comes from classical reversible circuits. These circuits are significantly weaker than AC0 and limited only to use of reversible gates (i.e. TOFFOLI and NOT). They are equivalent in power to bounded-read AC0 formulae, where each variable appears at most 2^{d} times.
In classical reversible circuits, each gate can only spread the influence of a bit to one other bit. Thus, in depth-d we can only compute FAN-OUT of size 2^{d}. Therefore, depth-\log n is necessary to perform FAN-OUT of size n.
In the context of decision problems, a QAC0 circuit without ancillae has roughly the same power as a mere classical reversible circuit. For uniformly random inputs, the state after each layer is maximally mixed (due to unitarity and uniform input distribution).
This was the key insight of [20], i.e., gates acting on many qubits are rarely active and can be removed with little error, thus enabling similar light-cone arguments to the classical reversible setting.
In QAC0 circuits with ancillae, a gate can use multiple ancillae such that all these ancillae become correlated with the input after the gate. However, even in the classical setting, there is a crucial distinction between the notions of FAN-OUT in AC0 circuits and in reversible circuits, in which a FAN-OUT operation is required to preserve reversibility.
Simply being entangled with many ancillae is not an indication of the latter since the input cannot be reliably recovered from a single ancilla alone.
Our techniques exploit this distinction. We observe that reversibility puts significant constraints on the type of computation that QAC0 circuits can perform. To our knowledge, these constraints cannot be bypassed with only polynomially many ancillae.
To uncover the true nature of their computation, it is crucial to study these circuits without severely limiting the number of ancillae, i.e., by considering their power with an arbitrary polynomial number of ancillae.
2.2 Setup
We define the output of a QAC0 circuit to be the output on a single designated register t, as in Section 2.2. We do not require any particular output state for qubits other than the output register t.
This is a weaker requirement than “clean-computation” or “dirty-computation” used in the prior works that establish an approximate depth-2 lower bound [24], making our results stronger. We find that, for fixed-depth circuits, relaxing the output requirement to a single register reveals more about the structure of the circuit’s computation of f.
{restatable*}
[Circuit computing classical function f]definitionqacoutput
Let C be a QAC0 circuit with a designated target register t and associated output basis \left(\ket{\mu_{0}},\ket{\mu_{1}}\right)
with \braket{\mu_{0}|\mu_{1}}=0. We say that C computes a Boolean function f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}, if
for all \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the output of C(\bm{x}) on t is exactly \ket{\mu_{f(\bm{x})}} and unentangled with other qubits.
Equivalently,
\forall\bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}\ \ \bra{\mu_{f(\bm{x})\oplus 1}}\cdot C(\bm{x})=0.
2.3 Depth-3 circuits cannot compute Parity or Majority
Our proof consists of several components that we detail below.
2.3.1 Block Diagonalization of Gates
All the multi-qubit classical reversible gates ( and and OR, composed with NOT) can be viewed as reflection gates. As shown by [24], this lets us define our gate set as reflections about arbitrary separable states.
For example, a Toffoli gate with controls on qubits in S and a target t is given by
(I-2\outerproduct*{\1}{\1}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{+}{+}_{t}).
Although reflection gates have no inherent “controls” and “target”, we can arbitrarily partition the qubits into controls and targets to view these gates as controlled unitaries as follows. For a gate given by G(S)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}), and any partitioning of qubits in G into two sets S=(X,Y), G can be diagonalized as follows,
\displaystyle G(S)=(I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{X})\otimes I_{Y}+\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{X}\otimes(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth})_{Y}
(3)
This can be interpreted as applying a smaller reflection, (I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth})_{Y}, on the targets Y, in the \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{X} subspace on the controls, and doing nothing to Y in the orthogonal subspace on the controls.
Additionally, these two subspaces are invariant under G(S) because any measurement on the qubits X in the \ket{\vec{\theta}} basis commutes with such a gate. Therefore, any projector that is either \outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{X} or orthogonal to \outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{X} commute with G and induces a unitary on Y.
For example, for any q\in S, and S^{\prime}=S\setminus q, conditioning on outcome \ket{\theta_{q}} on q gives,
\displaystyle\outerproduct*{\th_q}{\th_q}\cdot G(S)
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{\th_q}{\th_q}\otimes I_{S^{\prime}}-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}
(4)
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{\th_q}{\th_q}\otimes(I_{S^{\prime}}-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S^{\prime}})
(5)
\displaystyle=G(S^{\prime})\otimes\outerproduct*{\th_q}{\th_q}
(6)
Where G(S^{\prime}) is a valid reflection gate on the smaller subset S^{\prime}. Also, conditioning on outcome \ket{\theta^{\perp}_{q}} gives,
\displaystyle\outerproduct*{\th^\perp_q}{\th^\perp_q}G(S)
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{\th^\perp_q}{\th^\perp_q}\otimes I_{S^{\prime}}-2\underbrace{\outerproduct*{\th^\perp_q}{\th^\perp_q}\cdot\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}}_{=\braket{\theta_{q}|\theta^{\perp}_{q}}=0}
(7)
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{\th^\perp_q}{\th^\perp_q}\otimes I_{S^{\prime}}
(8)
Such measurements are unaffected by whether they are performed on the state before the gate or after. More generally, if the state of the qubits on S is either \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S} or some (possibly entangled) state orthogonal to \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S}, the gate only adds a global phase to the state and does not create any additional entanglement. The same can be said of any subset S^{\prime}\subseteq S that is in the state \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S^{\prime}}, the gate does not create any entanglement on qubits in S^{\prime}, but it may do so on qubits S\setminus S^{\prime}.
If a state on a subset of qubits S is denoted as \ket{\psi}_{S}, a pure state (as opposed to a mixed state \rho_{S}), then the qubits in S are not entangled with anything outside of S. For example, each single-qubit component of a fully separable state \ket{\vec{\theta}_{S}} is a pure state \ket{\theta_{q}} on qubit q\in S.
2.3.2 Quantum Analogue of Restrictions
A central building block of our depth-3 lower-bound is a new technique, referred to as the “clean-up step”.
This step applies “quantum restrictions" to simplify the first layer of gates in the circuit, such that each of them depends on at most 1 input qubit. We then show that for any cleaned-up circuit of depth-\leq 3, the circuit’s output can be simulated classically by a AC0 circuit whose size is polynomial in n.
Recall that a depth-d QAC0 circuit consists of d layers of gates on n input qubits, denoted by [n], and ancillae qubits A with |A|=\text{poly}(n). The reversibility property of the circuit enforces that each qubit appears in at most one gate per layer. As evidenced by classical techniques, such as the Switching Lemma [15], it is useful to ensure that all coordinates have disjoint light-cones in the bottom layer, i.e, each layer-1 gate contains at most one input qubit. Our clean-up step lets us simply convert any QAC0 circuit computing a Boolean function f that behaves well under restrictions (e.g., PARITY and MAJORITY) to one that computes f on a subset of at least n/3 coordinates, with the additional guarantee that each coordinate appears in at most one gate. This is reminiscent of clean-ups performed on AC0 circuits using random restrictions that simplify the first layer of gates.
As in [20], when analyzing QAC0 for approximate computation, we argue in our approximation lower bound that gates containing many input coordinates can be replaced by identity, while incurring a small error. However, this argument is not suitable for analysis of circuits with exact output, because the resultant circuit is no longer exact. In classical reversible circuits, however, this type of simplification can be achieved via deterministic restrictions, which preserve the exact computation. For instance, restricting a single coordinate of each layer-1  and gate to 0 kills the gate and leaves the rest of the coordinates unrestricted. This means that one can perform such a clean up on classical reversible circuits and leave at least half of the coordinates unrestricted (by restricting only coordinates from gates of width at least 2). However, since gates in a QAC0 circuit can be reflections about arbitrary separable states, we cannot always achieve this effect with a classical restriction.
Our technique, therefore, is a generalization of these deterministic restrictions for quantum circuits. The main idea is to restrict the input to a state lying in a subspace orthogonal to the gate’s reflection which, in effect, deactivates the gate. Additionally, we want to be able to apply these restrictions in QAC0. Finally, to ensure that the circuit still correctly outputs f(\bm{x}) after this quantum restriction, the restriction is specifically chosen to be a superposition of the classical restrictions that keep f(\bm{x}) invariant. For f=\texttt{PARITY} these are precisely the states formed by superpositions of classical restrictions of the same parity, and for f=\texttt{MAJORITY}, these are superpositions of classical restrictions with equal number of 0s and 1s.
We describe our clean-up step as the following lemma and defer its proof to Section 4.
{restatable*}[Clean-Up Lemma]lemmacleanup
Let C be a depth-d circuit that computes f(\bm{x}), where f(\bm{x}) is PARITY or MAJORITY, on n>2 coordinates with a separable ancilla starting state. Then, there is a depth-d circuit C^{\prime} that computes f(\bm{x}) on n/3 coordinates using a separable ancilla state and satisfies that every layer-1 gate of C^{\prime} contains at most 1 input qubit.
It turns out that performing this clean-up step gets us most of the way to an exact depth-2 lower bound, stated below as Corollary 2.1.
We note that [8] already provide a tighter bound, in terms of n, for PARITY in depth-2. Nevertheless, we include our alternative proof of Corollary 2.1 below, which also applies to MAJORITY and encompasses the main ideas used in Section 4 for the depth-3 bound.
Corollary 2.1 (Depth-2 Exact PARITY/MAJORITY Lower-Bound).
Let C be a n-input depth-2 QAC0 circuit with an arbitrary number of gates and ancillae, whose ancillae start in a separable state. Then, C cannot compute PARITY for n>6 or MAJORITY for n>12 coordinates.
Proof.
Suppose C computes f(\bm{x}) where f(\bm{x}) is PARITY or MAJORITY. Then, we can obtain a cleaned-up version of C that computes f(\bm{x}) on n^{\prime}\geq n/3 coordinates by applying Section 2.3.2. Now we will proceed to prove that a cleaned up circuit C on n inputs cannot compute PARITY for n>2 or MAJORITY for n>4.
Let G(S,t)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S,t}) be the final gate of C, containing the output register t.
We consider two cases depending on the state on S in C(\bm{x}):
Case 1:
If the state on S in C(\bm{x}) is always \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S}, regardless of the input, we can simplify G(S,t) to a single-qubit unitary on t. This results in a depth-1 circuit in which the light-cone of t contains a single coordinate. This cannot happen unless n=1, because the output of t does not depend on the other coordinates.
Case 2:
Otherwise, there is some qubit q\in S such that \outerproduct*{\pth_q}{\pth_q}\otimes I\cdot C(\bm{x}) is not always 0. Pick b such that, for the two qubit projector, \Pi_{q,t}:=\outerproduct*{\pth_q}{\pth_q}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}_{t}, the quantity \Pi_{q,t}\otimes I\cdot C(\bm{x}) is also not always 0. This is always possible because \outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}+\outerproduct*{\mu_0}{\mu_0}=I.
Letting C^{1} denote the depth-1 sub-circuit of C we have,
\displaystyle\Pi_{q,t}\otimes I\cdot G(s,t)\cdot C^{1}(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=\Pi_{q,t}\otimes I\cdot C^{1}(\bm{x})
(9)
Then, \Pi_{q,t} has at most two gates in its C^{1} light-cone and, thus, depends on at most two input coordinates (due to our cleanup).
Therefore, there exists a classical restriction R on these \leq 2 coordinates such that \Pi_{q,t}\otimes I\cdot C|_{R}(\bm{y})\neq 0 on all strings \bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n-|R|}. If C computes f(\bm{x}) correctly, it must be that f_{R}(\bm{y})=b is a constant function.
For PARITY this cannot happen when n-|R|>0 and for MAJORITY this cannot happen when n-|R|>2, regardless of the values R chooses for these (at most) 2 bits. Therefore, C cannot compute PARITY on n>2 coordinates or MAJORITY on n>4 coordinates.
∎
2.3.3 Classical Simulation of Shallow Quantum Circuits
For our depth-3 lower bound, we show that parts of the circuit can be simulated classically in the following sense. The circuit can be described as a unitary transformation on the 2^{n+|A|} dimensional space of the inputs and ancillae A. Since our ancillae start in a fixed state \ket{{\vec{0}}}_{A}, the state of the circuit at any point of the computation is restricted to lie in a smaller, rank 2^{n} subspace. Additionally, for circuits as in Section 2.2, the final state of the circuit fully lies in one of two orthogonal rank 2^{n-1} subspaces, determined by the classical function of the input. Extending this idea to other circuits,
for any projector \Pi and circuit C, we define a classical function f_{C,\Pi}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\} that captures whether or not C(\bm{x}) has a component in the +1 eigenspace of \Pi. We call this the activation function of \Pi on C.
That is,
f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})=[\Pi\cdot C(\bm{x})\neq 0]
where [\cdot] stands for the indicator of an event.
Observe that for any C that exactly computes a classical function f(\bm{x}) on a target register t in the {\ket{\mu_{0}},\ket{\mu_{1}}} basis, f_{C,\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x}) is precisely f(\bm{x}) and f_{C,\outerproduct*{\mu_0}{\mu_0}}(\bm{x}) is \neg f(\bm{x}). However, we don’t have an analogue of this for intermediate states of the circuit.
In general, it is possible for both f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})=1 and f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x})=1, and thus f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x}) does not always provide useful information. Our key observations, enabling us to use these activation functions effectively, are as follows.
At the start of the circuit, the entire input and ancillae state lies inside the subspace {\mathsf{S}}_{0}=\mathrm{span}\left(\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}\right)\otimes\mathcal{H}_{[n]}, where \mathcal{H}_{[n]} is the Hilbert space of our input qubits and \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A} is the ancillae starting state. Using the QAC0 normal form, originally proposed by [24], each gate G(S) of the QAC0 circuit is a reflection about a separable state \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S}. Observe that any state in the subspace {\mathsf{S}}_{\theta^{\perp}} that is orthogonal to \outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S} is unchanged by G(S). We show that the output of shallow circuits can simulated classically by tracking the evolution of the state in only a \text{poly}(n) number of such subspaces through their activation functions.
Building on these insights, we describe an AC0 circuit to simulate the activation function of the projector corresponding to the singular output of cleaned-up depth-3 QAC0 circuits. Our classical simulation of depth-3 QAC0 circuits with m ancillae produces a depth-3 \text{poly}(mn)-size AC0 circuit as stated in the theorem.
{restatable*}[Depth-3 Classical Simulation]theoremacsimthm
Let C be a single-output cleaned-up depth-3 QAC0 circuit on n inputs and m gates that computes the function f(\bm{x}) on n coordinates. Then, f(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(O(m^{4}\cdot n^{4}),3)
This is sufficient for a lower-bound against the usual setting of QAC0, which is limited to \text{poly}(n) gates, by applying known AC0 lower-bounds of [15]. We also present a stronger result Theorem 4.7 that rules out depth-3 QAC0 circuits for PARITY on more than O(1) coordinates with unlimited number of ancillae and gates. This is based on our observation that most of the activation functions in the lower layers of the circuit are monotone in the same direction, regardless of the number of gates, which enables us to construct a deterministic (classical) restriction simplifying most of the gates. In contrast, to simplify arbitrary AC0 circuits, we need to make use of random restrictions, which introduce a dependence on the circuit size. This monotonicity property does not necessarily hold at higher depths, and we expect the lower bounds at higher depths to depend on the size.
A consequence of Section 2.3.3 is that the activation functions at lower levels of QAC0 circuits can be simplified using random restrictions on the corresponding AC0 circuits. This provides evidence of a QAC0 analog of the Switching Lemma because the simplified activation functions are either a small junta or a CNF/DNF formula. Then, for polynomial-sized QAC0 circuits, we can potentially simplify the circuit itself using additional random restrictions.
2.4 Depth-2 QAC0  Circuits have O(\log n) Total Influence
We prove that any depth-2 QAC0 circuit C on n inputs has total influence O(\log n), regardless of the number of ancillae or gates. This is established by showing exponentially small Fourier tails: for any \varepsilon>0, the Fourier weight above level k=c\log(1/\eps)\log(n/\eps) is at most \varepsilon, where c is an absolute constant. Since PARITY has total influence n, this immediately implies an average-case depth-2 lower-bound against PARITY with unlimited ancillae, as well as any Boolean function with large total influence.11
1
Furthermore, since O(\log n)\ll n there exists a constant n such that any depth-2 QAC0 circuit cannot even approximately compute PARITY on n bits.
Comparison to Prior Work – Key Challenges and New Ideas.
We compare to prior work by Nadimpalli, Parham, Vasconcelos, and Yuen [20], which shows that any depth-d QAC0 circuit has small Fourier tails, but only for a restricted class of circuits with O(n^{1/d}) many ancillae. Our proof only holds in the more restricted depth-2 setting, but also in the more general unlimited ancillae setting. Nadimpalli et al. first proved their results for QAC0 circuits with no ancillae, and then applied a simple reduction to solve the case of O(n^{1/d}) many ancillae. We thus discuss the case of no ancillae as it is cleaner and easier to follow.
The total influence measures the average sensitivity of the circuit on a uniformly random input. On a random input, the initial state is the maximally mixed state, and since the circuit is reversible, the state is also the maximally mixed state after each layer. However, on the maximally mixed state, any CZ gate with fan-in \omega(\log n) is activated with negligible probability, and can thus be replaced by the identity gate while incurring only a small error in its Fourier tail. This leaves us with a circuit composed only of gates of fan-in O(\log n), meaning that the output depends only on a O(\log n)^{d} number of input qubits, and thus the total influence is at most O(\log n)^{d}.
This proof technique fails when we introduce ancillae since the state after each layer is no longer the maximally mixed state.
For example, consider the read-once DNF circuit for the TRIBES function, where \texttt{TRIBES}(x)=\lor_{i=1}^{s}\land_{j=1}^{w}x_{i,j} for w=\Theta(\log n) and s=\Theta(n/\log n). Note that, without loss of generality, we can apply controlled-OR and controlled- and gates (as they can be implemented using single-qubit gates before and after a CZ gate).
Any read-once DNF with s terms can be simulated by a depth-2 QAC0 circuit with s+1 ancillae, where in the first layer, each of the first s ancillae is flipped only if the corresponding term is true and in the second layer, the first s ancillae qubits are fed into a controlled-OR gate that flips the target ancilla qubit, that will contain the value of the DNF. In the case of the TRIBES function, we get s+1=O(n/\log n) ancillae.22
2
As this paragraph demonstrates, the TRIBES function can be implemented by depth-2 QAC0, and we see that the total influence of such circuits can be \Omega(\log n) as this is the total influence of the TRIBES function – proving the tightness of our total influence upper bound.
Observe though that the fan-in of the second layer is O(n/\log n), and nevertheless the gate is activated with constant probability on a uniformly random input. This is because after the first layer, the ancillae are quite “biased” towards \ket{0}, unlike in the case of a maximally mixed state.
Clearly, fan-in is not a good indicator of which gates are active with non-negligible probability in the presence of ancillae.
Håstad [15]
and Linial, Mansour, and Nisan [18] that use restrictions and the switching lemma to obtain Fourier tails of constant depth circuits. Generalizing the classical proof technique to the quantum setting has remained elusive, as the proofs rely heavily on the discreteness of the classical circuits where bits are either 0 or 1 and using encoding arguments (cf. Razborov’s proof of the switching lemma in Beame’s survey [4]).
We therefore need a novel technique.
We observe that the entropy of the mixed state entering a gate is a good indicator of which gates are active with non-negligible probability in the presence of ancillae, at least for the case of depth-2 circuits. Indeed, if the mixed state has a lot of entropy, and is also separable, then its “min-entropy” is large as well, which means that the state has negligible amplitude on any particular basis state. This means that the gate is activated with negligible probability. To use this approach, we need to: (i) reduce to the case of separable states entering a gate at layer 2, (ii) bound the total influence of the circuit assuming that the mixed state entering a gate has small entropy. We explain how to do this in the following. We believe that this approach can be extended to higher depths, but the main obstacle we face is that even for depth-3 circuits, the state entering a gate may not be separable, in which case it is unclear how to connect the entropy and min-entropy measures.
Proof Overview.
The proof proceeds in three main stages. First, we simplify the circuit structure by removing layer-1 gates that depend on too many input qubits. Specifically, any CZ gate at layer 1 depending on more than b=\Theta(\log(n/\eps)) input qubits can be replaced with the identity gate, incurring only \varepsilon/2 error in the Fourier tail. This is because such gates are rarely active on uniformly random inputs, and their removal changes the circuit’s behavior by at most O(2^{-b}) in \ell_{2} distance.
Second, we apply a random-valued restriction tailored to the circuit structure. For each remaining layer-1 gate that depends on between 1 and b input qubits, we randomly keep exactly one of its input qubits alive and fix the rest uniformly at random. Input qubits not involved in any gate remain alive. This restriction keeps alive at least n/b variables and reduces the Fourier tail analysis to structured circuits where each layer-1 gate depends on at most one input qubit (but potentially many ancillae).
Third, we analyze the Fourier tails of these structured circuits. Since the computation is single-output, we focus on the single layer-2 gate g containing the target qubit.
Allowing for the ancilla starting state to be an arbitrary product state, WLOG, g is a CZ gate that flips the phase when its input is \ket{1^{m}}. We partition the input qubits of g into disjoint sets Q_{0},Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{n}, where Q_{i} contains qubits from the layer-1 gate involving input x_{i} (if any), and Q_{0} contains qubits from ancilla-only gates. On input x, the mixed state entering g is \rho^{x}=\rho_{0}\otimes\rho_{1}^{x_{1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_{n}^{x_{n}}, where \rho_{i}^{b} is the state of Q_{i} when x_{i}=b, i.e., \rho^{x} is a highly separable mixed state.
The analysis splits into two cases based on the activation probability of gate g. Let \rho=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x}[\rho^{x}] be the average state over all inputs.
Case 1: If \bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}\leq\varepsilon/32, then gate g is almost always inactive. In this case, replacing g with identity changes the circuit’s acceptance probability function by at most \varepsilon/8 in \ell_{2} distance. The resulting circuit has only one layer of gates and computes a dictator function (depends on a single input), which has zero Fourier weight above level 1. This implies that the original circuit has at most \varepsilon/4 Fourier weight above level \Theta(\log(1/\eps)).
Case 2: If \bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}\geq\varepsilon/32, i.e., the gate is activated with non-negligible probability, then most \rho_{i}^{0},\rho_{i}^{1} are close to the the all 1s state. This implies that the trace distance between \rho_{i}^{0} and \rho_{i}^{1}, \mathrm{TD}(\rho_{i}^{0},\rho_{i}^{1}) is small, which implies that the influence in direction i is small and overall the total influence is small.
To get the exponential Fourier tail bound, we express the mixed state \rho as a “matrix Fourier decomposition”: First we express \rho_{i}^{x_{i}}=\rho_{i}+(-1)^{x_{i}}\cdot D_{i}, where D_{i}=(\rho_{i}^{0}-\rho_{i}^{1})/2 is the derivative with respect to x_{i} and \rho_{i}=\frac{1}{2}(\rho_{i}^{0}+\rho_{i}^{1}) is the average state. Then, we write the Fourier decomposition of the mixed state \rho^{x} as
\rho^{x}=\sum_{R\subseteq[n]}\widehat{\rho}(R)\cdot(-1)^{\sum_{i\in R}x_{i}}
where each \widehat{\rho}(R) is expressed as a product of the \rho_{i}’s (for i\not\in R) and D_{i}’s (for i\in R).
This decomposition is similar to a Fourier decomposition of Boolean functions except that the coefficients \hat{\rho}(R) are density matrices.
Then, we relate the Fourier coefficients of the acceptance probability function f_{C}(x) to those of \rho^{x}.
We show that for any set R\subseteq[n], we have |\widehat{f_{C}}(R)|\leq\|\widehat{\rho}(R)\|_{1}=\prod_{i\in R}\|D_{i}\|_{1}=\prod_{i\in R}\mathrm{TD}(\rho_{i}^{0},\rho_{i}^{1},). This implies that the Fourier weight at level \ell is at most (64\ln(8/\eps)/\ell)^{\ell} using Maclaurin’s inequality. Setting \ell=\Theta(\log(1/\eps)) ensures that {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq\ell}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon/4. Combining this with the errors from the simplification and restriction steps, we obtain the desired Fourier tail bound, which implies the O(\log n) total influence bound.
2.5 Depth-2 QAC0  Circuits Cannot Prepare Generalized Nekomatas
The proof techniques so far have focused on lower-bounds for computation of the PARITY function, which ultimately maps a variable input state into a single designated output target qubit. We will now describe our lower-bound techniques for preparation of a quantum state, which we refer to as a generalized nekomata, using a depth-2 QAC0 and unlimited ancillae.
For a QAC0 circuit synthesizing a quantum state such as a nekomatas, all qubits start in the fixed \ket{0} state, meaning there is no input. Thus, input-based restrictions are not possible and instead we “restrict” to certain subspaces by post-selecting on the output. Furthermore, rather than just a single output qubit, there are n target output qubits of interest. Whereas the final layer of a PARITY circuit trivially depends only on the singular gate acting on the sole output target, in a nekomata circuit O(n) gates can play a non-trivial role in the final layer by acting on all n output qubits and ancillae. Therefore, depth-2 lower bounds against nekomatas appear more challenging than those against PARITY.
Proof Sketch.
Although the state synthesis setting is fundamentally different from the input-output setting, this result follows the same core concepts behind our depth-3 bound. The proof consists of two parts.
Simplify final layer: Given a depth-d circuit that outputs a nekomata, we construct a separable state on some subset of qubits, \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q}, such that, inside the eigenspace of \outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}, (1) the final layer is simplified
(2) the state is still entangled across at least n/2 of the targets, and thus still a nekomata.
Structure after a single gate: Then, we argue that such a state cannot be created by a depth-2 circuit by reasoning about the entanglement structure of states created by depth-1 circuits. Since all the qubits start in the state \ket{{\vec{0}}}, qubits across different gates are unentangled, and we only need to consider a single gate. We observe that the state after a single (non-trivial) gate, (I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth})\cdot\ket{{\vec{0}}}, lies in a rank 2 subspace \mathrm{span}\{\ket{\vec{\theta}},\ket{{\vec{0}}}\} consisting of two non-orthogonal separable states. Additionally, for any partitioning of the qubits into targets T and ancillae A, it is the case that the state on T lies in \mathrm{span}\{\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{T},\ket{{\vec{0}}}_{T}\}, even when the state on A is restricted to lie inside some subspace of \mathcal{H}_{A}. The defining property of a generalized n-nekomata is that it has an n-partite rank 2 Schmidt decomposition. This is not possible for a state in \mathrm{span}\{\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{T},\ket{{\vec{0}}}\} unless |T|=n=2 because \braket{\vec{\theta}_{T}|{\vec{0}}}\neq 0.
2.6 Exact to approximate reduction for PARITY
Recently [12] showed that the previous approximate nekomata constructions, such as [24] can be made exact using the amplitude amplification of [14] [6], thus giving a \text{poly}(n) size QAC0 circuit for exact PARITY/FAN-OUT/MAJORITY on {\mathsf{polylog}}(n) qubits. We point out this allows us to eliminate the error in any QAC0 circuit that computes parity with at least 1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n) advantage on average, in the same asymptotic depth.
Theorem 2.2 (Approximate-to-Exact Parity in QAC0).
Let C be a depth-d QAC0 circuit with n input qubits and a ancillae.
Consider the function f_{C}:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to[0,1] defined by f_{C}(\bm{x})=\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\text{$C$ accepts $\bm{x}$}]. Let \rho\in[-1,1] be the correlation of f_{C}(\bm{x}) with \texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}), such that \rho=1/(\log n)^{\delta}. Then, there is a depth-O(d) circuit C^{\prime} using a\cdot n+n^{O(\delta)} ancillae that exactly computes \texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}) on every \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}.
The main approximate reduction from nekomata to PARITY, [24], requires the PARITY circuit to have error on most inputs rather than on average [24]. However, this can be easily remedied by using the “poor man’s cat state” that can be constructed in QNC0 [29] to map an input \bm{x} to a random input of the same parity as \bm{x}. Formally, this gives us the following.
Claim 2.3 (Average-to-Worst Case PARITY).
Let C be a depth-d QAC0 circuit with n input qubits and a ancillae and define f_{C}(\bm{x}) to be \mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\text{$C$ accepts $\bm{x}$}]. Let \gamma\in[-1,1] be the correlation between f_{C}(\bm{x}) and \texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}). Then, there is a depth-d^{\prime}=d+O(1) circuit C^{\prime} with a^{\prime}=a+O(n) ancillae such that, for every input \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the output register of C^{\prime}(\bm{x}) measures to \ket{\oplus_{\bm{x}}} with probability \geq 1/2+|\gamma|/2.
Then, using [24, 12] to create {\mathsf{polylog}}(n) many copies of the input register, we can obtain a circuit C with an arbitrarily low constant error. Finally, we use some standard ancilla tricks and then reflect about the state C\ket{+}^{\otimes n} to obtain a nekomata.
Claim 2.4 (Approximate-to-Exact nekomata).
Let C be a depth-d QAC0 circuit that constructs a state on n targets T using a ancillae, given by \ket{\psi}_{T,A}=C\ket{0^{a}}. Suppose that the qubits T have \geq 1/4 probability of measuring to 1^{n} and to 0^{n} each, then, there exists a circuit C^{\prime} of depth-d^{\prime}\leq 3(d+2) with a^{\prime}=a+1 ancillae that exactly synthesizes an n-nekomata, i.e.
C^{\prime}\cdot\ket{0^{a^{\prime}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0^{n}}\ket{\varphi_{0}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1^{n}}\ket{\varphi_{1}}
for some states \ket{\varphi_{0}},\ket{\varphi_{1}}.
We provide the formal proof of Theorem 2.2, which is a simple consequence of the aforementioned works in Appendix A. The proofs techniques we use in Section 4 and Section 6 rely on the circuit computation being exact. Nevertheless, extending these techniques to a higher depths would be sufficient to rule out approximate circuits for PARITY, MAJORITY and all related problems in QAC0.
3 Preliminaries
A depth d \mathsf{QAC} circuit acting on input qubits [n] and ancilla qubits A consists of d layers of multi-qubit Toffoli gates interleaved with layers of arbitrary single-qubit unitaries. The single-qubit unitaries are “free” and do not contribute to the depth.
Each qubit in the circuit can appear in at most one gate per layer, and therefore the layers with multi-qubit gates are associated with a partitioning of the qubits. The inputs start in the standard basis state \ket{\bm{x}} for \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n} and the ancillae start in the all \ket{{\vec{0}}} state.
Figure 1: QAC0 circuit computing f(\bm{x}). The circuit takes in a n-qubit classical input corresponding to the string \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}. Each ancilla starts in a fixed state \ket{0}. At the end of the circuit, the state on a designated output register contains the answer \ket{f(\bm{x})}. Each qubit can belong to at most one gate per layer and there are no locality based constraints on multi-qubit gates, thus, the illustrated circuit has depth 4.
There is an equivalent characterization of QAC0 due to [24] where all the single qubit unitaries are moved to a new layer at the end. The intermediate layers consist only of multi-qubit gates that reflect about product states and there are d such layers. A gate G acting on the subset of qubits S has the form,
\displaystyle G(S)=I_{S}-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S},
(10)
where \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S} is a separable state across all of S. Note that this gate is simply a reflection about the state \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S} and is a unitary with eigenvalues \pm 1.
We use the vector labels such as \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S} or \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{S} to denote a product state on S, whose component on any qubit q\in S is denoted by \ket{\theta_{q}} or \ket{\eta_{q}} respectively.
A depth d QAC0 circuit in this normal form therefore consists of d such layers and we assume that there are no extra single qubit unitaries in between. Additionally, we will consider single-output circuits, in which we allow the “output” to be in any basis and therefore do not need to consider the additional layer of single-qubit unitaries at the end of the computation. We define the output of such circuits as below.
\qacoutput
3.1 Additional Notation
We will use the shorthand notation C(\bm{x}) to refer to the state C\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}, the final state of circuit C on input \bm{x}, when the ancilla starting state \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A} is clear from the context.
For a classical restriction R, C_{|R} denotes the depth \leq d QAC circuit on n-|R| inputs given by fixing the inputs in R and treating them as ancillae.
For a distribution D we denote by x\sim D a sample from the distribution. Let X be a finite set. We denote by x\sim X a uniformly random sample from X.
We use the following notation while referring to the complexity of classical functions.
Definition 3.1 (AC0(s,d)).
AC0(s,d) refers to the set of all Boolean functions f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\} computable by classical AC0 circuits of depth d using at most s gates.
3.2 Analysis of Boolean Functions
For every function f:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}} there exists a unique Fourier representation
f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}{\hat{f}(S)}\cdot(-1)^{\sum_{i\in S}x_{i}}
where \hat{f}(S)\in{\mathbb{R}} are called the Fourier coefficients of f.
These coefficients satisfy
\hat{f}(S)=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}[f(x)\cdot\chi_{S}(x)]
for S\subseteq[n], where \chi_{S}(x)=(-1)^{\sum_{i\in S}x_{i}} are the Parity functions.
Indeed, one can see that the existence and uniqueness of the Fourier representation follows from the fact that the 2^{n} parity functions form an orthonormal basis to the space of all functions from {\{0,1\}}^{n} to {\mathbb{R}} equipped with inner product
\langle{f,g\rangle}=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[f(x)\cdot g(x)].
Parseval’s identity implies that
\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[f(x)^{2}]=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\hat{f}(S)^{2}
and both sides equal 1 if f is a Boolean function, i.e., f:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\}.
We define the total influence of f, {\mathbf{Inf}}[f], as
{\mathbf{Inf}}[f]=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\hat{f}(S)^{2}\cdot|S|.
(In the special case where f is a Boolean function, note that the Fourier coefficients squared of a Boolean function f naturally define a probability distribution over the sets \{S:S\subseteq[n]\} where set S is chosen with probability \hat{f}(S)^{2}. Then, the total influence is the expected size of S under this distribution.)
The total influence also equals the combinatorial quantity \sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{Inf}}_{i}[f], where {\mathbf{Inf}}_{i}[f] is the influence of the i-th coordinate on f defined as
{\mathbf{Inf}}_{i}[f]=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}\left[\left(\tfrac{|f(x)-f(x^{\oplus i})|}{2}\right)^{2}\right]\text{ where }x^{\oplus i}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1},\overline{x_{i}},x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{n}).
Note that if f is Boolean, then \tfrac{|f(x)-f(x^{\oplus i})|}{2}\in\{0,1\}, and its value indicates whether changing the i-th coordinate in x changes the value of f.
We say that a coordinate i is influential on f if {\mathbf{Inf}}_{i}[f]>0. We say that a function is a k-junta if at most k of its coordinates are influential (i.e., if f’s value depends on at most k coordinates). In other words, f is a k-junta if it can be written as a function g:\{0,1\}^{k}\to{\mathbb{R}} applied to some subset of k coordinates i_{1}<i_{2}<\dots<i_{k} as follows: f(x)=g(x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}).
We define the Fourier weight at level k, {\mathsf{W}}^{k}[f], and the Fourier tail at level k, {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f], as
{\mathsf{W}}^{k}[f]=\sum_{S:|S|=k}\hat{f}(S)^{2},\qquad{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f]=\sum_{S:|S|\geq k}\hat{f}(S)^{2}
A restriction is a partial assignment to the variables of a Boolean function. We denote it by a pair (J,z) where J\subseteq[n] is the set of coordinates that stay alive and z\in\{0,1\}^{[n]\setminus J} is an assignment to the rest. Given a function f:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}} and a restriction (J,z), we naturally get the restricted function f|_{J,z}:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}} defined by f|_{J,z}(x)=f(y) where for i\in[n], y_{i}=x_{i} if i\in J and y_{i}=z_{i} otherwise.
A random restriction is a distribution over restrictions. A random valued restriction is a distribution over restrictions of a special form – we first pick J\subseteq[n] from an arbitrary distribution and then pick z\in{\{0,1\}}^{[n]\setminus J} uniformly at random.
The expected Fourier coefficients under random valued restrictions are well understood.
Lemma 3.2 (Fourier weights under random valued restrictions).
Let f:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}}. Let J be a random subset of [n] under some arbitrary distribution D and let z\sim\{0,1\}^{[n]\setminus J}.
Then, for any set S\subseteq[n],
\displaystyle\mathop{\bf E\/}_{J,z}[\widehat{f|_{J,z}}(S)^{2}]=\sum_{T\subseteq[n]}\widehat{f}(T)^{2}\cdot\mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{J}[T\cap J=S].
(11)
In particular, for any k\in{\mathbb{N}},
\displaystyle\mathop{\bf E\/}_{J,z}[{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f|_{J,z}]]=\sum_{T\subseteq[n]}\widehat{f}(T)^{2}\cdot\mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{J}[|T\cap J|\geq k].
(12)
The proof was essentially given in [21, Prop. 4.17].
3.3 Trace Distance and its Properties
For two mixed states (density matrices) \rho,\sigma on the same Hilbert space, the trace distance is defined as
\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma)\;:=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\|\rho-\sigma\|_{1}\qquad\text{where}\quad\|X\|_{1}:=\mathrm{Tr}\sqrt{X^{\dagger}X}.
This metric has several important properties:
•
Range and equality: 0\leq\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma)\leq 1, and \mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma)=0 iff \rho=\sigma.
•
Unitary invariance: \mathrm{TD}(U\rho U^{\dagger},U\sigma U^{\dagger})=\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma) for any unitary U.
•
Tensoring: \mathrm{TD}(\rho\otimes\tau,\sigma\otimes\tau)=\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma) for any fixed \tau.
•
Triangle inequality: \mathrm{TD}(\rho,\tau)\leq\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma)+\mathrm{TD}(\sigma,\tau).
•
Contractivity under channels and measurements:
Let \Phi be any quantum channel. Then for all density matrices \rho,\sigma,
\mathrm{TD}\bigl(\Phi(\rho),\,\Phi(\sigma)\bigr)\;\leq\;\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma).
In particular, if \mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma)\leq\varepsilon, then the outputs \Phi(\rho) and \Phi(\sigma) are also \varepsilon-close in trace distance.
Hence no quantum operation or measurement can increase the statistical distance beyond \varepsilon.
3.4 Activation Functions
We will refer to activation functions of projectors on intermediate states of our circuit, described by the corresponding sub-circuit. These are defined below.
Definition 3.3 (Projector Activation Function).
Given a QAC0 circuit C on n inputs and any projector \Pi_{S} acting on a subset of qubits S, the activation function of \Pi_{S} on C is a classical Boolean function, f_{C,\Pi_{S}}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\} defined as.
f_{C,\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x}):=\left[\Pi_{S}\cdot C(\bm{x})\neq 0\right]
where the notation \left[\cdot\right] to refers to an indicator function.
We note that it is possible for both f_{C,\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x})=1 and f_{C,(I-\Pi_{S})}(\bm{x})=1, but it cannot be that both of them are 0. For a projector \Pi, we will use \mathrm{eig}(\Pi) to refer to the +1 eigenspace of \Pi. Then, the activation function is essentially checking if C(\bm{x}) has a component in \mathrm{eig}(\Pi).
3.4.1 Projectors and their Eigenspaces
We give some useful lemmata for manipulating projectors.
Lemma 3.4 (Projector Decomposition).
Let \Pi be a projector on a Hilbert space \mathcal{H} that can be decomposed as \Pi=\left(\bigotimes_{i=0}^{n}\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}\right)
where B_{i} is a set of qubits.
Then
1.
\mathrm{eig}(\Pi)=\bigotimes_{i=0}^{n}\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}).
2.
\mathrm{eig}(I-\Pi)=\mathrm{span}\{\bigcup_{i=0}^{n}\mathrm{eig}(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})\}.
Proof.
1.
The first item follows as any +1 eigenvector of \Pi is the tensor product of +1 eigenvectors for \Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}.
2.
All these projectors can be simultaneously diagonalized because they form a set of commuting observables, i.e,
[(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}),(I-\Pi)]=0 and [(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}),(I-\Pi^{j}_{B_{j}})]=0 for all i,j\in[n]. Take any eigenvector \ket{v} from this diagonalization. If \ket{v} is a +1 eigenvector of (I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}) for some i, then it is a 0 eigenvector of \Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}} and \Pi, and thus a +1 eigenvector of (I-\Pi). If \ket{v} is a 0 eigenvector of every (I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}), then from (1), it must be a +1 eigenvector of \Pi, and thus a 0 eigenvector of (I-\Pi).
∎
Lemma 3.5.
Suppose \mathrm{eig}(\Pi)=\mathrm{span}\{\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{(i)}\})) for some set of projectors \Pi^{(i)}. Then,
any state \ket{\psi} that has a component inside \mathrm{eig}(\Pi) must have a component inside one of the subspaces \mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{(i)}), and vice versa,
i.e., \Pi\ket{\psi}\neq 0 if and only if \exists i\in I
such that \Pi^{(i)}\ket{\psi}\neq 0.
Proof.
In one direction, suppose that \Pi^{(i)}\ket{\psi}\neq 0 for some i.
Then, \ket{\psi} has a non-zero inner product with a +1 eigenvector of \Pi^{(i)} which is also an +1 eigenvector of \Pi, so we get that \Pi\ket{\psi}\neq 0.
In the other direction, if \Pi^{(i)}\ket{\psi}=0 for all i, then \ket{\psi} is orthogonal to \mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{(i)}) for all i and it must be orthogonal to their span, which is \mathrm{eig}(\Pi), thus \Pi\ket{\psi}=0.
∎
3.5 Nekomata States
Definition 3.6 (Generalized n-nekomata).
A state \ket{\psi} is said to be a generalized n-nekomata if, for some \alpha\neq 0,\beta\neq 0, it has the form,
\ket{\psi}=\alpha\cdot\ket{\mu_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}
where \braket{\mu_{i}|\mu^{\perp}_{i}}=0 for i\in[n].
Here A is the set of remaining qubits referred to as the ancillae of \ket{\psi} and the qubits t_{1},t_{2}\dots t_{n} are as the targets of \ket{\psi}.
A nekomata, as defined in the literature, has \alpha=\beta=1/\sqrt{2} and \ket{\mu_{i}}=\ket{0}, and is included in the above definition.
Definition 3.7 (Generalized nekomata under separable post-selection (GNSP)).
A state \ket{\varphi} is said to be a generalized n-nekomata under separable post-selection, if for some (possibly empty) subset of qubits Q and a separable state \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q}, \outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\varphi} is nonzero and a (un-normalized) n-nekomata. In other words, for some set of n target qubits T,
\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\varphi}=\alpha\cdot\ket{\mu_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}
where \alpha\neq 0,\beta\neq 0 and \braket{\mu_{i}|\mu^{\perp}_{i}}=0.
Then any generalized n-nekomata is also a k-GNSP for any k\leq n.
4 Depth-3 QAC0  Circuits Cannot Compute PARITY or MAJORITY
In this section, we will prove that depth-3 QAC0 circuits cannot compute PARITY or MAJORITY. We will first show a reduction from circuits computing PARITY or MAJORITY to circuits whose first layer is “cleaned up” in the sense that each gate depends on at most one input qubit. We will then show that any cleaned-up depth-3 QAC0 circuit cannot compute PARITY or MAJORITY. To do that, we will show that any cleaned-up depth-3 QAC0 circuit can be simulated classically in AC0.
4.1 The Clean-Up Lemma
We begin with the proof of the clean-up lemma which is restated below.
\cleanup
Proof.
Note that PARITY is invariant under any classical restriction and MAJORITY is invariant under any balanced classical restriction with an equal number of 0s and 1s among the fixed coordinates.
Our goal is to convert the layer-1 gates of the circuit into “cleaned up” gates that depend on at most one input qubit.
We handle all the other gates as follows:
Handling Gates with exactly 2 input qubits.
Suppose that there are m such gates, with 2m total coordinates. Apply a balanced classical restriction R on 2\lceil m/2\rceil\leq m+1 coordinates, by fixing one coordinate from each gate, and potentially one extra coordinate in case m is odd (to ensure we fix an even number of coordinates and maintain a balanced restriction). We thus restrict at most (m+1)/2m\leq 2/3 fraction of the coordinates. The balanced restriction ensures that the output of the resulting circuit is correct.
Handling Gates with 3 or more input qubits.
Let G(S) be any such gate. We describe our quantum analogue of a restriction that turns two input qubits from S\cap[n] to ancillae and deactivates G(S).
Applying such a restriction for every gate with at least 3 input qubits deactivates all these gates, while preserving at least 1/3 fraction of the input qubits.
Pick any two input coordinates in i,j\in S\cap[n], say (i,j)=(1,2) and convert them to ancilla by hard-wiring their state to \ket{\varphi}_{1,2} satisfying (i)
\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}:=\alpha\cdot\ket{01}+\beta\cdot\ket{10} and (ii) \braket{\vec{\theta}_{1,2}|\varphi}=0.
Such a state exists because the dimension of the space of states spanned by \ket{01} and \ket{10} is 2 and \braket{\vec{\theta}_{1,2}|\varphi}=0 is a linear constraint, so there must exist a non-trivial solution.
More explicitly, we choose \alpha=\frac{a}{\sqrt{|a|^{2}+|b|^{2}}} and \beta=\frac{-b}{\sqrt{|a|^{2}+|b|^{2}}} for a=\braket{\vec{\theta}_{1,2}|10} and b=\braket{\vec{\theta}_{1,2}|01} if (a,b)\neq(0,0) and otherwise choose \alpha=1 and \beta=0.
This restriction deactivates G because \braket{\vec{\theta}_{1,2}|\varphi}=0.
We will first argue that the output of the circuit under this restriction still computes PARITY or MAJORITY (resp.) and then reason about the resulting circuit. Let \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A} denote the original ancilla state, so that, on input \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n-2}, the resulting circuit produces the state C\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}. Also, let \left\{\ket{\mu_{0}},\ket{\mu_{1}}\right\} denote the original output basis of C.
C computes PARITY.
Observe that \ket{\phi_{1,2}} is a superposition over two classical restrictions setting the coordinates (1,2) to either 01 or 10 respectively, and that both of these restrictions flips the parity of the input.
Thus, for all \bm{x}, C\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}} correctly outputs PARITY according to Section 2.2 in the basis (\ket{\nu_{0}},\ket{\nu_{1}}) for \ket{\nu_{b}}=\ket{\mu_{b\oplus 1}} (i.e., we flip what we consider to be 0 and 1 in the output basis to accomdoate the fact that we flipped the parity of the input by restricting to \ket{\phi_{1,2}}).
More slowly, for b=\texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}), we have that
\displaystyle\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}
\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\cdot\ket{01\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\ket{10\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}=0.
(13)
C computes MAJORITY.
Here, we observe that \ket{\phi_{1,2}} is a superposition over two classical restrictions setting the coordinates (1,2) to either 01 or 10 respectively, and that both of these restrictions maintains the majority of the input.
Thus, for all \bm{x}, C\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}} correctly outputs MAJORITY according to the same basis (\ket{\mu_{0}},\ket{\mu_{1}}) as before.
More slowly, for b=\neg\texttt{MAJORITY}(\bm{x}), we have that
\displaystyle\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}
\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\cdot\ket{01\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\ket{10\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}=0.
(14)
So far, we have shown that the circuit’s output under this restriction still computes PARITY or MAJORITY. However, we need to implement the restriction in the standard model with separable initial ancilla state without increasing the depth of the circuit, as we explain next.
Converting back to separable ancillae.
Let D be the depth-d sub-circuit consisting of gates other than G(S), so that,
C=D\cdot G(S).
The new linear operator on the inputs is given by,
\displaystyle C\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}
\displaystyle=D\cdot G(S)\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}
(15)
\displaystyle=D\cdot(I-\underbrace{2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth})\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}}_{=0}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}
(16)
\displaystyle=D\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}
(17)
Here the ancilla starting state is not necessarily separable because \ket{\varphi}_{1,2} could be entangled. To fix this, we add a new gate G^{\prime}(t_{1},t_{2}) in place of G to compute \ket{\varphi}_{1,2} from a separable state. One such gate is given by G^{\prime}=\mathtt{CNOT}(1,2) with the starting state \ket{\mu}_{1}\ket{1}_{2}, where \ket{\mu}_{1}=\alpha\ket{0}+\beta\ket{1}. Then,
\displaystyle G^{\prime}\cdot\ket{\mu}_{1}\ket{1}_{2}
\displaystyle=\mathtt{CNOT}(1,2)\cdot\left(\alpha\ket{01}+\beta\ket{11}\right)
(18)
\displaystyle=\alpha\ket{01}+\beta\ket{10}
(19)
Since the first layer in D doesn’t apply any gate on (1,2),
the new circuit C^{\prime\prime}=D\cdot G^{\prime} is still a depth-\leq d circuit on the other input coordinates with a separable initial ancilla state \ket{\vec{\eta}}\ket{\mu}_{1}\ket{1}_{2}.
So far, we explained how to clean up one gate with at least 3 input qubits.
Repeating this transformation for all layer-1 gates containing \geq 3 coordinates in the original circuit preserves at least 1/3 fraction of these coordinates.
Figure 2: Clean-up of a gate G with more than 3 input qubits. The restriction fixes the state of \ket{x_{i}}\ket{x_{j}} to \ket{\varphi}_{i,j} in a way that deactivates the gate G. Then, the restriction to \ket{\varphi}_{i,j} is equivalent to applying a CNOT gate on the separable initial ancillae state \ket{\mu}\ket{1}.
The classical and quantum restrictions together fixes at most 2n/3 input qubits and converts them to ancillae, such that the resulting circuit acts on at least n/3 coordinates and has at most one input qubit per layer-1 gate, i.e., a cleaned-up circuit.
∎
From here on, we will assume that the circuits we consider are cleaned-up. Recall that, for a QAC0 circuit C and projector \Pi acting on some of its qubits, the activation function f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x}), defined in Section 3.4, checks whether C(\bm{x}) has a component in the non-zero eigenspace of \Pi (i.e., \mathrm{eig}(\Pi)). We will show that at each layer of the circuit (which is of depth-3), the relevant activation functions can be simulated in AC0.
We demonstrate this in the following sections.
4.2 AC0  Simulation of Projectors After Layer One
After the clean-up in Section 2.3.2, the state after the first layer of the circuit is separable across all input qubits, and has the following form,
\displaystyle C(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=\ket{\psi_{0}}_{B_{0}}\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{i\in[n]}\ket{\psi_{i}(x_{i})}_{B_{i}}\right)
(20)
where \ket{\psi_{i}(x_{i})}_{B_{i}} is a state on qubits B_{i} in layer-1 gate containing input qubit i, that only depends on x_{i}, and \ket{\psi_{0}}_{B_{0}} is a fixed state on the remaining ancillae.
In this section, we show that the activation functions of certain projectors have a simple form that lets us simulate them classically. These consist of two main building blocks: (i) projectors with few gates in their light-cones (“juntas”), described in Definition 4.1 and (ii) projectors that are separable across all the B_{i}’s from Equation 20.
The first two lemmas show that the activation functions of these two building blocks can be simulated classically in AC0 depth-(\leq 2).
Definition 4.1 (Junta Projector).
Given a depth-1 QAC0 circuit C, a projector \Pi_{S} acting on a subset of qubits S is a k-junta projector on C if at most k gates in C act on some qubit from S.
Lemma 4.2 (Junta Projector in AC0).
Let C be a cleaned-up depth-1 QAC0 circuit on n inputs and \Pi_{S} be a k-junta projector on C. Then, f_{C,\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x}) is a k-junta.
In particular, f_{C,\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x}) can be implemented by a width k DNF formula with at most 2^{k} clauses.
Proof.
Let C^{\prime} be the sub-circuit that only contains the gates in the light-cone of S (i.e., the gates that contain a qubit from S). Then, C^{\prime} acts on at most k coordinates and f_{C,\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x})=f_{C^{\prime},\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x}). This shows that f_{C,\Pi_{S}} is a k-junta, and it is straightforward to see that any k-junta can be written as a width k DNF with at most 2^{k} clauses. (Each clause will check that the value of the k junta variables equals a specific value for which the function should output 1.)
∎
Lemma 4.3 (Separable Projector in AC0).
Let C be a cleaned-up depth-1 QAC0 circuit on n inputs whose ancillae start in \ket{{\vec{0}}}_{A}. Let \Pi be projector that has the form,
\Pi=\Pi^{0}_{B_{0}}\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}\right)
where B_{i} is the set of qubits in G_{i}, the layer-1 gate containing i\in[n] and B_{0}\subseteq A is the set of remaining ancillae.
(note that \Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}} could in particular be I_{B_{i}} as this is a special case of a projector.)
Then, the following holds.
1.
f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(n,1), and is either a constant function or given by,
f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{n}f_{C,\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}}(x_{i})
2.
f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(n,1), and is either the constant function or given by,
f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x})=\bigvee_{i=1}^{n}f_{C,(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})}(x_{i}).
Proof.
First, note that for any projector \Pi^{\prime}_{B_{0}} acting only on the ancilla B_{0}, f_{C,\Pi^{\prime}_{B_{0}}}(\bm{x}) is input independent.
From Item (1) of Lemma 3.4, \Pi\cdot C(\bm{x})\neq 0 iff \Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}\cdot C(\bm{x})\neq 0 for every i. Therefore,
\displaystyle f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=\bigwedge_{i=0}^{n}f_{C,\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}}(\bm{x})
(21)
and from Lemma 4.2 each f_{C,\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}}(\bm{x}) for i\in[n] depends only on x_{i}. Hence, this function is either 1 or given by an  and gate on the variables x_{1},\dots x_{n} and their negations.
This completes the first part of the proof.
We continue to prove the second item.
From Lemma 3.4, we have that,
\displaystyle\mathrm{eig}(I-\Pi)
\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}\left\{\mathrm{eig}((I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})\otimes I_{\overline{B_{i}}})\right\}_{i\in\{0,\dots,n\}}
(22)
Then, by Lemma 3.5, any state \ket{\psi} that has a component inside \mathrm{eig}(I-\Pi) must have a component inside one of the subspaces \mathrm{eig}((I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})\otimes I_{\overline{B_{i}}}), and vice versa.
This gives,
\displaystyle f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=\bigvee_{i=0}^{n}f_{C,(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})}(\bm{x})
(23)
and then Lemma 4.2 shows that for i\in[n], f_{C,(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})}(\bm{x}) is depends only on the variable x_{i}. Hence, this function is either always 1 or is given by an OR gate on the variables x_{1},\ldots,x_{n} or their negations.33
3
An alternative argument goes as follows:
f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x})=\left[(I-\Pi)\cdot C(\bm{x})\neq 0\right]=\neg\left[(I-\Pi)\cdot C(\bm{x})=0\right]=\neg\left[C(\bm{x})\in\mathrm{eig}(\Pi)\right].
Now, for C(\bm{x}) to be a +1 eigenstate of \Pi it must be a tensor product of +1 eigenstates of \Pi_{B_{i}}^{(i)} for i\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}. Hence, the condition of C(\bm{x})\in\mathrm{eig}(\Pi) can be rewritten as an AND function on the literals x_{1},\neg x_{1}\ldots,x_{n},\neg x_{n}, and by De Morgan’s law, f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x}) can be written as an OR function on the same literals.
∎
Corollary 4.4 (Combinations of Separable Projectors AC0).
Let C be a depth-1 cleaned up QAC0 circuit with ancillae in \ket{{\vec{0}}}_{A} and \Pi_{T} be a projector that is given by the product of k+1 projectors,
\Pi_{T}=\Pi^{0}_{T_{0}}\otimes\Pi^{1}_{T_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\Pi^{k}_{T_{k}}
satisfying, \Pi^{0}_{T_{0}}=\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{T_{0}} and \Pi^{j}_{T_{j}}=I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{T_{j}} for j\in[k] for some separable states \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{T_{0}},\ldots,\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{T_{k}}.
Then, f_{C,\Pi_{T}}(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(O(n^{k+1}),2) and is a n-DNF formula with (n+1)^{k} clauses.
Proof.
