Let B_{i} be the set of qubits in the layer 1 gate containing input qubit i and B_{0} be the set of remaining ancillae. For i\in[0,n],j\in[k], define projector \mathcal{Q}^{(i,j)} acting on B_{i}\cap T_{j} as,
\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}^{(i,j)}:=\begin{cases}0\ \ \ \text{if }B_{i}\cap T_{j}=\emptyset\\
I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{B_{i}\cap T_{j}}\ \ \ \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
(24)
Then, since (I-\Pi^{j}_{T_{j}})=\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{T_{j}}, we can apply Lemma 3.4 to get,
\displaystyle\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{j}_{T_{j}})
\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}\left\{\mathrm{eig}\left({\mathcal{Q}^{(i,j)}\otimes I_{T_{j}\setminus B_{i}}}\right)\right\}_{i\in[0,n]}.
(25)
Now, for a tuple \bm{z}\in[0,n]^{k}, define the following projector,
\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(\bm{z}):=\bigotimes_{j\in[k]}\mathcal{Q}^{(z_{j},j)}.
(26)
Combining with Equation 25 gives,
\displaystyle\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{1}_{T_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\Pi^{k}_{T_{k}})
\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}\left\{\mathrm{eig}(\mathcal{P}(\bm{z}))\right\}_{\bm{z}\in[0,n]^{k}}
(27)
\displaystyle\Rightarrow\mathrm{eig}(\Pi_{T})
\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}\left\{\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{0}_{T_{0}}\otimes\mathcal{P}(\bm{z}))\right\}_{\bm{z}\in[0,n]^{k}}.
(28)
Therefore, from Lemma 3.5,
\displaystyle f_{C,\Pi_{T}}(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=\bigvee_{\bm{z}\in[0,n]^{k}}f_{C,\Pi^{0}_{T_{0}}\otimes\mathcal{P}(\bm{z})}(\bm{x})
(29)
By definition \mathcal{P}(\bm{z}) is separable across all the B_{i}s for i\in[0,n] and so is \Pi^{0}_{T_{0}}\otimes\mathcal{P}(\bm{z}). Therefore, from Lemma 4.3, each f_{C,\Pi^{0}_{T_{0}\otimes\mathcal{P}(\bm{z})}}(\bm{x}) is a width \leq n  and function and taking an OR of (n+1)^{k} of them gives f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(O(n^{k+1}),2).
∎
4.3 AC0  Simulation of Projectors After Layer Two
Consider a depth-2 circuit C=L^{(2)}\cdot L^{(1)} whose depth-1 sub-circuit is given by L^{(1)}. A projector \Pi_{S} that is a k junta-projector on L^{(1)} may not necessarily have a small light-cone in C, making it challenging to simulate its activation function. In the case that \Pi_{S} is also a k junta-projector on the depth-1 sub-circuit formed by L^{(2)}, we can break it up into the building blocks from Section 4.2 to simulate its activation function. As it turns out, this is sufficient for the purpose of simulating the output of depth-\leq 3 circuits (see Section 4.4 for the proof).
Lemma 4.5 (Layer-2 Small Projector).
Let C=L^{(2)}\cdot L^{(1)} be a cleaned up depth-2 QAC0 circuit on n inputs and \Pi_{T} be a projector on a subset of qubits T. Suppose that \Pi_{T} is a k-junta projector on both the depth-1 circuits L^{(1)} and L^{(2)}, formed by the gates in layers 1 and 2 of C respectively. Then,
f_{C,\Pi_{T}}(\bm{x}) can be written as a DNF of size at most O(4^{k}\cdot n^{k+1}).
Proof.
The depth-1 sub-circuit formed by L^{(1)} can be partitioned into D_{1}\otimes D_{2}, where D_{1} is the sub-circuit formed by \leq k layer-1 gates on T, and D_{2} contains the remaining gates.
Assume without loss of generality that L^{(2)} contains only the \leq k gates G_{1}(S_{1})\dots G_{k}(S_{k}), in the light-cone of T (as the remaining gates can be replaced with identity, not affecting the output of the circuit).
First, we partition each S_{j} into X_{j},Y_{j} where X_{j}=S_{j}\setminus T and Y_{j}=S_{j}\cap T and define,
\displaystyle X:=\bigcup_{j\in[k]}X_{j},
(30)
\displaystyle Y:=\bigcup_{j\in[k]}Y_{j}
(31)
Then, X\cup T belongs to the same set of layer-1 and layer-2 gates as T, so we will proceed assuming without loss of generality that X\subseteq T by extending \Pi_{T}\to\Pi_{T}\otimes I_{X\setminus T} to act on X\cup T.
By the Heisenberg evolution of \Pi_{T}\otimes I_{Y} acting on C to \widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y}=(L^{(2)})^{\dagger}\Pi L^{(2)} acting on L^{(1)},
\displaystyle f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})=f_{L^{(1)},\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y}}(\bm{x})
(32)
Hence, it is sufficient to show that f_{L^{(1)},\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y}}\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}. We will do so by decomposing \widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y} into the building blocks from Section 4.2.
For each G_{j}(S_{j}), treating Y_{j} as the controls and X_{j} as the targets (ref. Section 2.3.1) gives,
\displaystyle G_{j}(S_{j})
\displaystyle:=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S_{j}})
(33)
\displaystyle=(I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{Y_{j}})\otimes I_{X_{j}}+\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{Y_{j}}\otimes\underbrace{(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{X_{j}})}_{G_{j}(X_{j})}
(34)
We will describe below the block-diagonalization of \widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y}=(L^{(2)})^{\dagger}\Pi L^{(2)} into 2^{k} subspaces corresponding to the subspaces of \mathcal{H}_{Y}. We will then argue that, inside each subspace, \widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y} is separable across T,Y and its component on T is a k-junta projector, while its component on Y has the form in Corollary 4.4.
Define \mathcal{Q}^{(1)}_{Y_{j}}=\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{Y_{j}} and \mathcal{Q}^{(0)}_{Y_{j}}=I-\mathcal{Q}^{1}_{Y_{j}} for each j\in[k]. Then, Equation 34 becomes,
\displaystyle G_{j}(S_{j})
\displaystyle=\mathcal{Q}^{(0)}_{Y_{j}}\otimes I_{X_{j}}+\mathcal{Q}^{(1)}_{Y_{j}}\otimes G_{j}(X_{j})
(35)
and for both values of b\in\{0,1\},
\displaystyle[\mathcal{Q}^{(b)}_{Y_{j}},G_{j}(S_{j})]
\displaystyle=0
(i.e., the commutator is 0.)
\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}^{(b)}_{Y_{j}}\cdot G_{j}(S_{j})
\displaystyle=\mathcal{Q}^{(b)}_{Y_{j}}\otimes\underbrace{(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{X_{j}})^{b}}_{G_{j}(X_{j})^{b}}
(36)
where, for a unitary U, U^{0}=I and U^{1}=U and [O_{1},O_{2}] denotes the commutator of two operators O_{1},O_{2}. Then, we identify each subspace by a k-bit string \bm{y}. For each \bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{k}, the projector onto this subspace, \mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})_{Y}\otimes I_{X}, is given by,
\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}({\bm{y}})_{Y}
\displaystyle:=\bigotimes_{j\in[k]}\mathcal{Q}^{y_{j}}_{Y_{j}}
(37)
Due to Equation 36, [\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y}),L^{(2)}]=0. Then, L^{(2)} inside this subspace is a unitary U(\bm{y}) on X given by,
\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})\cdot L^{(2)}
\displaystyle=\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{j\in[k]}(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{X_{j}})^{y_{j}}\right)
(38)
\displaystyle=\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})\otimes U(\bm{y})_{X}
(39)
Putting it all together, we can block-diagonalize \widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y} as,
\displaystyle\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y}
\displaystyle=(L^{(2)})^{\dagger}\Pi_{T}L^{(2)}
(40)
\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{k}}\underbrace{U(\bm{y})^{\dagger}\cdot\Pi_{T}\cdot U(\bm{y})}_{\mathcal{P}(\bm{y})_{T}}\otimes\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})_{Y}
(41)
\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{k}}\mathcal{P}(\bm{y})_{T}\otimes\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})_{Y}
(42)
where each \mathcal{P}(\bm{y}) is a projector only on T. Therefore,
\displaystyle f_{C,\Pi_{T}}(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=f_{D_{1}\otimes D_{2},\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y}}(\bm{x})
(43)
\displaystyle=\bigvee_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{k}}f_{D_{1}\otimes D_{2},\mathcal{P}(\bm{y})\otimes\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})}(\bm{x})
(44)
\displaystyle=\bigvee_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{k}}\left(f_{D_{1},\mathcal{P}(\bm{y})_{T}}(\bm{x})\bigwedge f_{D_{2},\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})_{Y}}(\bm{x})\right)
(45)
Since \mathcal{P}(\bm{y})_{T} only acts on D_{1}, it is a k-junta projector and can be implemented by a DNF of size at most 2^{k}+1 according to Lemma 4.2. Also, from Corollary 4.4, f_{D_{2},\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})} can be implemented by a DNF of size at most O(n^{k+1}).
The AND of two DNFs of size s_{1} and s_{2} can be written as a DNF of size s_{1}\cdot s_{2} whose terms are all pairwise ANDs of all pairs of terms in the original DNFs. Therefore, f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x}) can be written as a DNF of size at most O(4^{k}\cdot n^{k+1}).
∎
4.4 AC0  Simulation of cleaned-up depth-3 circuits
Now we have all the pieces to prove Section 2.3.3.
\acsimthm
Proof.
Suppose that C computes a function f(\bm{x}) with n coordinates (for large enough n) on register t in the \ket{\mu_{b}} basis. Then, f_{C,\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})=f(\bm{x}).
Let G(S,t)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S,t}) be the final (layer-3) gate on t and let D be the depth-2 sub-circuit. Since other layer-3 gates do not affect the output on t, without loss of generality, we can assume that C=G\cdot D (i.e., there are no other layer-3 gates other than G).
Let \theta^{\perp}_{S}=(I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}) and \ket{\widetilde{\mu_{b}}}=(I_{t}-2\outerproduct*{\th_t}{\th_t})\cdot\ket{\mu_{b}} for b\in\{0,1\}. Consider the following function,
\displaystyle g(\bm{x})=\begin{cases}f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x}),&\text{ if }f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})=1\\
f_{D,\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}}(\bm{x}),&\text{ otherwise }\end{cases}.
(46)
It is sufficient to argue that: (1) g(\bm{x})=f_{C,\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})=f(\bm{x}) and (2) g(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(O(m^{4}\cdot n^{4}),3).
Proof of (1).
Recall from Section 2.3.1 that we can treat t as the “target” and S as the controls in G to decompose it as:
\displaystyle G(S,t)
\displaystyle=\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes I_{t}+\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}\otimes(I_{t}-2\outerproduct*{\th_t}{\th_t})
(47)
We will show that the output of g(\bm{x}) is correct for each of the two cases in Equation 46 (i.e., for the case f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})=1 and its complement).
The Case f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})=1:
In this case \theta^{\perp}_{S}\cdot D(\bm{x})\neq 0.
Then, there must exists a b\in\{0,1\} such that \theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}\cdot D(\bm{x})\neq 0, because \outerproduct*{\mu_0}{\mu_0}_{t}+\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}_{t}=I_{t}.
This means that f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}}(\bm{x})=1 for some b\in\{0,1\}.
On the other hand, \theta^{\perp}_{S} deactivates G, i.e., \theta^{\perp}_{S}\cdot G=\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes I_{t}, and thus for any b\in\{0,1\},
\displaystyle\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}\cdot C=\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}\cdot D.
(48)
In particular for b=\neg f(\bm{x}) the LHS of the above equation equals 0 and thus f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}}(\bm{x})=0.
Overall, we have shown that f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}}(\bm{x})=1 for exactly one b\in\{0,1\}, and this b must be f(\bm{x}). Therefore, in the case f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})=1, we have f(\bm{x})=f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x}).
The Case f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})=0:
In this case,
\theta^{\perp}_{S}\cdot C(\bm{x})=\theta^{\perp}_{S}\cdot D(\bm{x})=0, since \theta^{\perp}_{S} deactivates G.
Recall that f_{C,\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})=f(\bm{x}).
When we project C(\bm{x}) onto \outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}_{t} we get
\displaystyle\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}_{t}\cdot C(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=((\theta^{\perp}_{S}+\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S})\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}_{t})\cdot C(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=(\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}_{t})\cdot C(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=(\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}_{t})(\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes I_{t}+\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}\otimes(I_{t}-2\outerproduct*{\th_t}{\th_t}))\cdot D(\bm{x})
(Using Equation 47)
\displaystyle=(\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}\otimes(\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}_{t}\cdot(I_{t}-2\outerproduct*{\th_t}{\th_t})))\cdot D(\bm{x})
and by denoting \ket{\widetilde{\mu_{1}}}=(I_{t}-2\outerproduct*{\th_t}{\th_t})\cdot\ket{\mu_{1}},
\displaystyle(I_{t}-2\outerproduct*{\th_t}{\th_t})\cdot\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}_{t}\cdot C(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=(\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}_{t})\cdot D(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=(\theta^{\perp}_{S}+\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S})\otimes\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}_{t})\cdot D(\bm{x})
(Since \theta^{\perp}_{S}\cdot D(\bm{x})=0)
\displaystyle=(I_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}_{t})\cdot D(\bm{x})
and thus in this case, f(\bm{x})=f_{C,\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})=f_{D,\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}}(\bm{x}).
Proof of (2).
By Part (1), we have that
\displaystyle g(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=\left(f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})\bigwedge f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})\right)\bigvee\left(\neg f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})\bigwedge f_{D,\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}}(\bm{x})\right)
(49)
so it suffices to show that each of the three activation functions can be implemented in AC0.
Let m_{1},m_{2} be the number of layer 1 and 2 gates respectively and for \ell\in[2],j\in[m_{\ell}], let B_{\ell,j} denote the set of qubits in the jth gate at layer \ell. Let B_{\ell,0} denote the set of qubits in layer \ell without any gates. To apply Lemma 4.5, we will first partition the qubits of S into subsets that belong to at most one gate per layer.
For 0\leq i\leq m_{1} and 0\leq j\leq m_{2}, define S_{ij} as,
\displaystyle S_{ij}=B_{1,i}\cap B_{2,j}\cap S
(50)
Recall that \theta^{\perp}_{S}=(I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}), and let \theta^{\perp}_{S_{ij}}:=(I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S_{ij}}). For S_{ij}=\emptyset, we define \theta^{\perp}_{S_{ij}} to be the 0 projector. Then, from Lemma 3.4
\displaystyle\mathrm{eig}(\theta^{\perp}_{S})
\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}{\left\{\mathrm{eig}(\theta^{\perp}_{S_{ij}}\otimes I_{S\setminus S_{ij}})\right\}}_{i\in\left[0,m_{1}\right],\ j\in\left[0,m_{2}\right]}
(51)
\displaystyle\mathrm{eig}(\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}_{t})
\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}{\left\{\mathrm{eig}(\theta^{\perp}_{S_{ij}}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}_{t}\otimes I_{S\setminus S_{ij}})\right\}}_{i\in\left[0,m_{1}\right],\ j\in\left[0,m_{2}\right]}
(52)
From Lemma 3.5,
\displaystyle f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=\bigvee_{i\in\left[0,m_{1}\right],\ j\in\left[0,m_{2}\right]}f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S_{ij}}}(\bm{x})
(53)
\displaystyle f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}}(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=\bigvee_{i\in\left[0,m_{1}\right],\ j\in\left[0,m_{2}\right]}f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S_{ij}}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}}(\bm{x}).
(54)
By definition \theta^{\perp}_{S_{ij}} contains qubits from at most one gate per layer.
Then, due to Lemma 4.5, both these functions can be implemented by DNFs of size O(n^{2}m^{2}).
Finally, the function f_{D,\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}}(\bm{x}) can be implemented by a DNF of size O(n^{2}) since it is a 1-junta projector on both the depth-1 and depth-2 sub-circuits. Overall,
\displaystyle g(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=\left(f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})\bigwedge f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})\right)\bigvee\left(\neg f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})\bigwedge f_{D,\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}}(\bm{x})\right)
(55)
can be implemented as a depth-4 AC0 circuit of O(m^{2}\cdot n^{2}) size.
A slightly more careful analysis, explained next, shows that the depth is actually 3.
We show how to implement Equation 55 by an OR-AND-OR circuit of size O(m^{4}n^{4}). As the AND of two DNFs of size at most O(n^{2}m^{2}), the left hand side \left(f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})\bigwedge f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})\right) can be implemented as a DNF of size O(m^{4}n^{4}), which is a special case of OR-AND-OR circuit.
As for the right hand side, the expression \neg f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x}) can be implemented by a CNF of size O(n^{2}m^{2}) due to De Morgan’s law, which is an AND of O(n^{2}m^{2}) clauses. Furthermore,
the expression f_{D,\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}}(\bm{x}) can be implemented by a DNF of size O(n^{2}).
Finally, the AND of a CNF of size s_{1} and a DNF of size s_{2} can be written as a OR-AND-OR circuit of size O((s_{1}+n)\cdot s_{2}) as follows.
Suppose \phi=C_{1}\land\dots\land C_{s_{1}} and \psi=T_{1}\lor\dots\lor T_{s_{2}} are CNF and DNF formulas respectively where each clause C_{i} is an OR of literals and each term T_{j} is an AND of literals. Then, the AND of \phi and \psi can be written as a OR-AND-OR circuit of size O(s_{1}\cdot s_{2}) as follows.
\displaystyle\phi\land\psi
\displaystyle=(C_{1}\land\dots\land C_{s_{1}})\land(T_{1}\lor\dots\lor T_{s_{2}})
\displaystyle=\bigvee_{i=1}^{s_{2}}(C_{1}\land\dots\land C_{s_{1}}\land T_{i})
which is a OR-AND-OR circuit of size O(s_{1}\cdot s_{2})
as (C_{1}\land\dots\land C_{s_{1}}\land T_{i}) is a CNF with at most s_{1}+n clauses as the term T_{i} is an AND of at most n literals, a special case of a CNF of size n.
∎
Corollary 4.6 (depth-3 Sub-exponential Lower Bound).
Let C be a single-output cleaned up depth-3 QAC0 circuit C on n inputs with m=\exp(o(\sqrt{n})) gates that computes the function f(\bm{x}) on n coordinates. Then, f(\bm{x}) cannot be the PARITY or MAJORITY function.
Proof.
First, we apply the clean-up step from Section 2.3.2 while keeping at least n^{\prime}=n/3 coordinates.
Then, by Section 2.3.3, f(\bm{x}) is a function that can be computed by a depth-3 AC0 circuit of size O(m^{4}\cdot n^{4}). Based on the known AC0 lower-bound of [15], if f(\bm{x}) is either PARITY or MAJORITY, it requires m^{4}n^{4}\geq\exp(\Omega(\sqrt{n})), making m\geq\exp(\Omega(\sqrt{n})).
∎
4.5 Size-independent depth-3 Lower-Bound for PARITY
Recall that if C computes f(\bm{x}) on target t in (\ket{\mu_{0}},\ket{\mu_{1}}) basis, f_{\outerproduct*{C,\mu_u}{C,\mu_u}}(\bm{x})=f(\bm{x}) and Section 2.3.3 gives an AC0 circuit for this function for such depth-\leq 3 cleaned up circuit C. We will use the fact that PARITY is invariant under any classical restriction to construct a specific \leq 2n/3 qubit restriction to simplify this AC0 circuit.
For a circuit C and projector \Pi, we say that \Pi kills C if \Pi\cdot C(\bm{x})=0 for all \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}. Similarly, we say that a classical restriction R kills a boolean function f(\bm{x}) if f|_{R}(\bm{x})=0 for all \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n-|R|}. For activation functions, note \left(f_{C,\Pi}\right)|_{R}(\bm{x})=f_{C|_{R},\Pi}(\bm{x}).
For any layer 2 gate G(S)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}) of a depth-2 circuit C, we use the notation f_{C,G}(\bm{x}) to refer to the activation function f_{C,\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}}(\bm{x}). Then, since f_{C,\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}}(\bm{x})=f_{C^{1},\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}}(\bm{x}), where C^{1} is the depth-1 sub-circuit of C, it follows from Lemma 4.3 that either f_{C,G}(\bm{x})=1 for all \bm{x} (trivial) or it is the  and function on a subset of the variables. Then, we have the following two key observations.
{restatable*}
[Limited non-monotonicity]lemmaonesidedmono
Let C be a cleaned up depth-2 circuit on n>2 inputs. Then, there exists a string z\in\{0,1\}^{n}, such that for each i\in[n], the single-coordinate restriction R=(i,z_{i}) kills f_{C,G} for at most two layer-2 gates G with non-trivial activation function.
{restatable*}
[Single-qubit activation functions at depth-2]lemmasingleqbadproj
Let C be a cleaned-up depth-2 circuit and \outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q} be a projector that does not kill C. Let, G=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}) be the layer 2 gate containing q. Then, at least one of the below must hold.
1.
Either there is a restriction R on |R|\leq 2n/3 coordinates that fixes f_{C|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}}(\bm{x})=1 for all \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n-|R|},
2.
Or f_{C,\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}}(\bm{x})=f_{C,G}(\bm{x}) and is given by an  and function (up to NOT gates) of width at least 2n/3.
These are sufficient to prove our main theorem and we defer their proofs to the next section.
Theorem 4.7 (Depth-3 Lower-Bound with Unlimited Ancillae).
Let C be a depth-3 \mathsf{QAC}^{0} circuit on n=\omega(1) coordinates and an arbitrary number of ancillae and size, that computes the function f(\bm{x}). Then f(\bm{x}) cannot be the PARITY function.
Proof.
Suppose for contradiction that f(\bm{x}) is PARITY.
First we will perform the cleanup step from Section 2.3.2, which preserves at least n/3=\omega(1) coordinates. Now we will proceed to prove the bound against cleaned up circuits on n coordinates.
To do so, we will construct a restriction that preserves \Theta(n) qubits and simplifies the final gate on the target qubit t. From Section 2.3.1, the final gate on t, G(S,t)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth_{S,t}}{\vth_{S,t}}) can be viewed as a controlled-U gate on target t as below.
\displaystyle G(S,t)
\displaystyle=\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes I_{t}+\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}\otimes(I_{t}-2\outerproduct*{\th_t}{\th_t})
(56)
Then, we will argue that there is a restriction to either guarantee that we are always in the \theta^{\perp}=(I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}) subspace, in which G is inactive, or guarantee that we are orthogonal to the subspace, which simplifies G into a single qubit unitary.
First we will remove all the redundant qubits from the gates, these are the qubits that are always in the state \ket{\theta}_{q} regardless of the input, making \outerproduct*{\pth_q}{\pth_q} kill C. Now WLOG S contains no such qubits. We will use C^{2} to denote the sub-circuits consisting of gates up to layer 2.
Restrict to identity subspace.
Suppose that there is a qubit q\in S such that \ket{\eta}_{q}=\ket{\theta^{\perp}_{q}} satisfies point (1) of Section 4.5, i.e., there exists a restriction R on at most 2n/3 coordinates to fix f_{C^{2}|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}}(\bm{x})=1. Then, C|_{R} still correctly computes f(\bm{x}) on \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n-|R|} in some basis \left(\ket{\mu_{0}},\ket{\mu_{1}}\right) on t. Since \outerproduct*{\mu_0}{\mu_0}+\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}=I, f_{C^{2}|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}}(\bm{x}) is nonzero for some value of b\in\{0,1\}.
Additionally, for b=f(\bm{x})\oplus 1, f_{C|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}}(\bm{x})=0.
Hence,
\displaystyle f_{C^{2}|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=f_{C|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}\ \ \ \ \ \ \ (\text{due to }\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}\cdot G=\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}\otimes I)
(57)
\displaystyle=f(\bm{x}).
(58)
However, from Lemma 4.5, f_{C^{2}|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(O(n^{3}),2). From the known bounds of [15] for AC0 circuits, this is a contradiction to n=\omega(1).
No restriction to identity subspace.
This is when the previous case doesn’t apply. Let H_{1}\dots H_{m} be the layer-2 gates containing at least one qubit from S. Then, for every qubit q\in S belonging to the layer 2 gate H_{j}, Section 4.5 gives that
f_{C^{2},\outerproduct*{\pth_q}{\pth_q}}(\bm{x})=f_{C^{2},H_{j}}(\bm{x}) and is a width \geq 2n/3  and function.
Now we will argue that there is a restriction R on \leq 0.9n inputs, that makes f_{C^{2}|_{R},H_{j}}(\bm{x})=0 for all \bm{x}. This has the effect of
making f_{C^{2}|_{R},\outerproduct*{\pth_q}{\pth_q}}(\bm{x})=0 for all q\in S forcing the state on S after C^{2} to be \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S} regardless of input. Then, from Equation 56, this simplifies G(S,t) to a single qubit unitary acting only on t, giving us a depth-\leq 2 circuit computing parity on n^{\prime}\geq 0.1n coordinates.
We will use Section 4.5 to construct R. The idea is that the activation function corresponding to all but a O(1) number of these gates is monotone in the same direction for a large fraction of the inputs. This allows us to construct a restriction that kills all these gates simultaneously while handling O(1) other gates separately.
For each gate H_{j} with j\in[m], define \mathcal{K}(H_{j}) to be the set of all single coordinate restrictions that kill f_{C^{2},H_{j}}, i.e.,
\displaystyle\mathcal{K}(H_{j}):=\left\{(i,b):\forall\bm{x}\ \ f_{C^{2}|_{(i,b)},H_{j}}(\bm{x})=0\right\}_{i\in[n],b\in\{0,1\}}
(59)
Recall that each f_{C^{2},H_{j}}(\bm{x}) is an  and of \geq 2n/3 literals, which implies \left\lvert\mathcal{K}(H_{j})\right\rvert\geq 2n/3.
First, let \mathcal{B} be the set of all the gates H_{j} for j\in[m] such that \mathcal{K}(H_{j}) contains at least 0.1n elements of the form (i,z_{i}), where z_{i} is defined according to Section 4.5. Then, from Section 4.5, \left\lvert\mathcal{B}\right\rvert\leq 2n/0.1n\leq 20, and each \left\lvert\mathcal{K}(H_{j})\right\rvert>20. By picking a coordinate (i,z_{i})\in\mathcal{K}(H_{j}) from each H_{j} in \mathcal{B}, this gives a restriction R_{0} on \leq 20 qubits that kills all these gates in \mathcal{B} simultaneously.
Let R_{1} be a restriction on arbitrary 3/4n inputs not in R_{0}, such that each i in R_{1} is set to x_{i}=z_{i}\oplus 1. We will argue that R_{1} kills all the gates H_{j} outside \mathcal{B}.
Then, R=R_{1}\cup R_{0}.
Every gate in \mathcal{B} is killed in C^{2}|_{R} due to R_{0}. Now, for every gate H_{j}\not\in\mathcal{B}, \mathcal{K}(H_{j}) contains at least 2/3n-0.1n>0.5n elements of the form (i,z_{i}\oplus 1). Since R_{1} leaves only 0.25n elements unfixed, there is at least one such element from \mathcal{K}(H_{j}) in R_{1}.
Therefore, R is such that f_{C|_{R},H_{j}}(\bm{x})=0 for all j\in[m] and \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n-|R|}.
Furthermore, |R|\leq|R_{0}|+|R_{1}|\leq 0.75n+20\leq 0.8n, for n large enough. Hence, C|_{R} is a depth-2 circuit that computes parity on \geq 0.2n inputs and it must be that 0.2n\leq 6 due to Corollary 2.1.
∎
4.5.1 Intermediate proofs
Now we provide the proofs of the two lemmas.
\onesidedmono
Proof.
For each i, let \ket{\theta^{1}_{i}} be the component of i corresponding to its layer 1 gate G_{i}=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth^1}{\vth^1}_{A_{i},i}) containing the ancillae A_{i}.
We will set z_{i}=\theta^{1}_{i} if \ket{\theta^{1}_{i}}\in\left\{\ket{0},\ket{1}\right\} or z_{i}=0 otherwise. For any layer 2 gate G=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth^2_S}{\vth^2_S}) acting on qubits S, we will argue that (i,z_{i}) kills f_{C,G}(\bm{x}) only if either i\in S or A_{i}\subseteq S. Then, this implies that there can be at most two layer 2 gates that are killed by (i,z_{i}).
Note that since measurements corresponding to layer 2 reflections commute with layer 2 gates, we have that f_{C,G}(\bm{x})=f_{C^{1},\outerproduct*{\vth^2}{\vth^2}_{S}}, where C^{1} is the layer 1 sub-circuit.
Additionally, by the assumption that f_{C,G}(\bm{x}) is non-trivial and from Lemma 4.3, we have that any (i,b) kills f_{C,G}(\bm{x}) if and only if it kills f_{G_{i},\outerproduct*{\vth^2}{\vth^2}_{S}}(\bm{x}), where G_{i} here denotes the circuit consisting only of the layer-1 gate acting on i.
Consider the case when i\not\in S and A_{i}\not\subseteq S. We consider the mixed state of G_{i}(z_{i}) on A_{i}\cap S.
This is obtained by measuring qubits i and A_{i}\setminus S in any basis, so in particular, we measure them according to \theta^{1}. We note that (i) if we measure \ket{\theta^{1}_{a}} for all a\in A_{i}\setminus S and \ket{\theta^{1}_{i}} for i, then the remaining gate is a non-trivial reflection gate on A_{i}\cap S. Denote the result of this gate on the ancillae A_{i}\cap S by \ket{\psi}. (ii) Otherwise, the remaining gate is identity on A_{i}\cap S. By definition of z_{i} and the fact that we assumed that layer-1 gates are non-trivial, i.e., that \braket{\theta^{1}_{a}|0}\neq 0 for any ancilla a starting in \ket{0}, we get that we are in case (i) with non-zero probability. By the fact that we assumed that layer-1 gates are non-trivial, i.e., that \left\lvert\braket{\theta^{1}_{a}|1}\right\rvert\neq 1 for any ancilla a, we get that we are in case (ii) with non-zero probability. We see that in the two cases we got different vectors, so the Schmidt rank of the mixed state is 2.
Since f_{C,G} is non-trivial, \outerproduct*{\th^2_{S}}{\th^2_{S}} does not kill G_{i}, and so it must be that for at least one of the two vectors v\in\{\ket{0},\ket{\psi}\} we have \outerproduct*{\th^2_{S}}{\th^2_{S}}\cdot v\neq 0. This means that with non-zero probability we get in G_{i}(z_{i}) a state that is not killed by \outerproduct*{\th^2_{S}}{\th^2_{S}}, and thus (i,z_{i}) does not kill f_{G_{i},\outerproduct*{\vth^2}{\vth^2}_{S}}.
The remaining cases, i\in S or A_{i}\subseteq S, can happen for at most two such layer-2 gates. Therefore, (i,z_{i}) can kill f_{C,G} for at most two layer-2 gates G.
∎
\singleqbadproj
Proof.
We will prove the lemma by considering f_{C^{1},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}}(\bm{x}) where C^{1} is the depth-1 sub-circuit.
The case when \outerproduct*{\eta_q}{\eta_q} kills C^{1}.
It must be the case [\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q},G]\neq 0, since \outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q} doesn’t kill C, making \braket{\eta_{q}|\theta_{q}}\neq 0.
Then, on any input \bm{x},
\displaystyle\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}\cdot C(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}\cdot(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth^2_S}{\vth^2_S})\cdot C^{1}(\bm{x})
(60)
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}\cdot(-2\outerproduct*{\vth^2_S}{\vth^2_S})\cdot C^{1}(\bm{x})
(61)
\displaystyle=-2\ket{\eta}_{q}\ket{\vec{\theta}^{2}}_{S\setminus q}\cdot\braket{\eta_{q}|\theta_{q}}\cdot\left(\bra{\vec{\theta}^{2}_{S}}\cdot C^{1}(\bm{x})\right)
(62)
and thus, f_{\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}}(\bm{x})=f_{C,\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}}(\bm{x})=f_{C,G}(\bm{x}).
Since f_{C,\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}}(\bm{x})=f_{C^{1},\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}}(\bm{x}), it follows from Lemma 4.3 that f_{C,\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}}(\bm{x}) is an  and gate of width w\leq n. If w\leq 2n/3 then we have our restriction R by fixing all the coordinates to satisfy the gate. Otherwise, w\geq 2n/3 as required.
The case when \outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q} does not kill C^{1}.
If f(\bm{x})=f_{C,\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}}(\bm{x}) is a 2-junta, then since \outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q} doesn’t kill C, there is a restriction on the \leq 2 coordinates that f(\bm{x}) depends on that makes it always 1.
Otherwise, if f(\bm{x}) is not a 2-junta there are at least two input-dependent layer 1 gates in the light-cone of \outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}. Then, there must be a qubit r that doesn’t share layer 1 gates with \outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q} such that \outerproduct*{\pth_{r}}{\pth_{r}} does not kill C^{1}. This is because we can remove any “redundant qubits", i.e., qubits that are always in the \ket{\theta}_{r} state before G, until we are either left with a small light-cone or find such an r.
Then, for \Pi=\outerproduct*{\pth_r}{\pth_r}\otimes\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}, f_{C^{1},\Pi} is given by Lemma 4.3 and by assumption, is not the constant function 0. Additionally, f_{C^{1},\Pi}(\bm{x}) is a 2-junta. Then, observe that for all \bm{x},
\displaystyle\Pi\cdot G(S)\cdot C^{1}(\bm{x})
\displaystyle=\Pi\cdot C^{1}(\bm{x})
(63)
Therefore, f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})=f_{C^{1},\Pi}(\bm{x}) and we can let R be the restriction that fixes this 2-junta to 1.
∎
5 Depth-2 QAC0  Circuits Have Small Total Influence
In this section, we will prove that any depth-2 QAC0 circuit has small total influence, as defined in Section 3.2. In particular, we will show that, regardless of the number of ancillae, the total influence of an n-input depth-2 QAC0 circuit is upper-bounded by O(\log n).
To establish this, we will prove a stronger bound on the Fourier concentration (showing exponentially small Fourier tails) of the circuit’s outcome as a function of the input qubits.
Since PARITY has total influence n, this implies that the functions computable by depth-2 QAC0 circuits have small correlation with PARITY. Therefore, this result offers a novel average-case depth-2 lower-bound against PARITY \in QAC0 with unlimited ancillae. More generally, the result implies an average-case depth-2 lower-bound against any Boolean function with large total influence.
5.1 Main Proof
We will now prove the main result of this section, showing that for any depth-2 QAC0 circuit C, the Fourier tail of the function f_{C}(x)=\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\text{$C$ accepts $x$}] at level k=c\log(1/\eps)\log(n/\eps) is at most \varepsilon, i.e. {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon. Along the way, we will introduce several intermediate claims and lemmata that will be proved in Section 5.2. The formal theorem statement is as follows.
Theorem 5.1.
There exists a constant c\geq 1 such that the following holds. Let C be a depth-2 QAC0 circuit with n input qubits and any number a of ancilla qubits.
Consider the function f_{C}:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to[0,1] defined by f_{C}(x)=\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\text{$C$ accepts $x$}]. Then, for any \varepsilon>0,
\displaystyle{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k(\varepsilon)}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon,\quad\textnormal{ where }\;k(\varepsilon)=c\log(1/\eps)\log(n/\eps)
(64)
Proof of Theorem 5.1.
We will give an overview of the full proof with reference to several intermediate claims and lemmata. We defer the proofs of these intermediate results to Section 5.2.
We begin the proof by simplifying the CZ gates at layer 1 of the circuit, i.e., those closest to the inputs.
We replace each gate that depends on many input qubits with the identity gate (incurring a small error) and then apply a random restriction tailored to the circuit structure. The purpose of these two steps is to reduce to a more structured case, where each gate at layer 1 depends on at most one input qubit (but potentially many other ancillae). Moreover, we show that these steps behave well with respect to the Fourier tails of the circuit.
Reduction to a Structured Circuit.
We consider the gates at layer 1. Recall that in QAC0, gates at a certain layer are non-overlapping. This means that for each of the layer-1 gates, g_{1},\dots,g_{\ell}, there is a set of incoming input bits, S_{1},\dots,S_{\ell}\subseteq[n], such that S_{1},\dots,S_{\ell} are disjoint (where possibly some of the S_{i} are empty sets, as the corresponding gates only depend on ancillae).
We first show that any gate g_{i} whose corresponding S_{i} contains more than b\triangleq\log(16n/\eps) inputs can be replaced with the identity gate, while incurring smalle error. In particular, Claim 5.2 shows that replacing each such gate with identity changes f_{C} by at most \varepsilon/2n in Fourier weight above level k.
Since there are at most n such gates (because each gate depends on at least one input qubit and the gates are non-overlapping), the Fourier weight above level k differs by at most \varepsilon/2.
Claim 5.2.
Let g be a CZ-gate at layer 1 with input qubits S\subseteq[n] entering it. Let C^{\prime} be the circuit where g is replaced with identity.
Then \|f_{C}-f_{C^{\prime}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq 4\cdot 2^{-|S|}.
Furthermore, for any k, the Fourier weight above level k of f_{C} and f_{C^{\prime}} differs by at most
\displaystyle|{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]-{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C^{\prime}}]|\leq 8\cdot 2^{-|S|}.
(65)
Random Restrictions.
We replace C with a circuit C^{\prime}, replacing the above mentioned layer-1 gates that depend on more than b input qubits with identity, and continue to analyze the Fourier tails of f_{C^{\prime}}.
Each layer-1 gate of f_{C^{\prime}} depends on at most b input qubits. We will apply a random-valued restriction that randomly picks at most one input qubit per gate keeping it alive and sets the remaining inputs uniformly at random. The random restriction will sample a random subset J\subseteq[n] of the variables to stay alive, based on the circuit structure, and a partial assignment z\in\{0,1\}^{[n]\setminus J} sampled uniformly at random.
We will now describe the explicit random restriction process for sampling J. We consider only the gates g_{i} for which 1\leq|S_{i}|\leq b (recall that b=\log(16n/\eps)). For each such gate, we pick exactly one of the bits in S_{i} to be included in J uniformly at random and independently of all other choices. Input qubits not involved in any gate always remain alive. Claim 5.3 demonstrates that Fourier tails behave nicely with respect to this random restriction.
(Observe that this restriction always keeps at least n/b variables alive.)
Claim 5.3.
Let b\in{\mathbb{N}} and S_{1},\dots,S_{\ell}\subseteq[n] be disjoint sets of size between 1 and b.
Define S_{0}=[n]\setminus(S_{1}\cup\dots\cup S_{\ell}) so that S_{0},\ldots,S_{\ell} form a partition of [n].
Consider the random valued restriction (J,z) that for each i\in\{1,\ldots,\ell\}, picks independently uniformly at random exactly one element from to S_{i} to J, and furthermore surely picks all elements in S_{0} to J.
Then, for any k\in{\mathbb{N}} and function f:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}}, the above random restriction process satisfies
\displaystyle{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq 4kb}[f]\leq 2\cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{J,z}[{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f|_{J,z}]].
(66)
Fourier Tail Bounds for Structured Circuits.
With Claim 5.3, the proof of Theorem 5.1 is thus reduced to proving Fourier tail bounds of the structured depth-2 QAC0 circuits, which we denote C^{\prime\prime}, with layer-1 gates each depending on at most one input qubit (and potentially many ancillae).
Specifically, it remains to prove that for any such circuit C^{\prime\prime}, {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C^{\prime\prime}}]\leq\varepsilon/4 for k=\Theta(\log(1/\eps)).
While the circuit C^{\prime\prime} depends only on the variables in J that were kept alive, it will be convenient to think of it as a circuit with n input qubits as well, where qubits outside J are ignored. Without loss of generality, since the computation is single-output, we only need to consider the single layer-2 gate, g, containing the target qubit. Also, since the ancilla starting state is allowed to be an arbitrary separable state, without loss of generality, the gate g is a CZ gate which flips the phase iff the input is \ket{1^{m}}, where m is the number of input qubits to g.
We partition the input qubits of g into disjoint sets Q_{0},Q_{1},Q_{2},\ldots,Q_{n} where for i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, Q_{i} is a set, potentially empty, of the qubits involved with the layer-1 gate containing x_{i} and Q_{0} contains the qubits coming from ancilla-only layer-1 gates. Note that for any fixed input x\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the states for these different subsets are separable.
We will now impose that the input to the layer-2 gate g is a mixed state. Specifically, any layer-1 qubit which is not contained in g will be traced out.
Let \rho_{0} be the mixed state of qubits in Q_{0}. For i\in[n], let \rho_{i}^{b} be the mixed state of the qubits in Q_{i} when x_{i}=b, for b\in\{0,1\}.
(If Q_{i}=\emptyset then \rho_{i}^{b}=(1), the trivial mixed state of dimension one, for both b\in\{0,1\}.)
Then, on input x\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the state entering g is
\displaystyle\rho^{x}=\rho_{0}\otimes\rho_{1}^{x_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\rho_{n}^{x_{n}}.
(67)
We will denote the average state over the two options for x_{i} as
\displaystyle\rho_{i}=\frac{1}{2}(\rho_{i}^{0}+\rho_{i}^{1})
(68)
and the average state over all 2^{n} options for x as \rho, where we note that
\displaystyle\rho=\rho_{0}\otimes\rho_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes\rho_{n}.
(69)
We will divide the remainder of the proof into two main cases. First, we consider the case in which the layer-2 gate is almost always inactive, meaning g can be replaced by identity without notably affecting the acceptance probability on most inputs. In this case, the resultant function is close to a dictator function (i.e. depends only on one input qubit) and has extremely small Fourier tails. In the second remaining case, we argue that the “entropy” of the incoming state to the gate is small. This turns out to imply that the function’s total influence and Fourier tails are small.
Case 1: g is almost always inactive.
Suppose \bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}\leq\varepsilon/32.
For each fixed x, let \varepsilon_{x}:=\bra{1^{m}}\rho^{x}\ket{1^{m}}. Then, \mathop{\bf E\/}_{x}[\varepsilon_{x}]=\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}\leq\varepsilon/32
and for each fixed x, Lemma 5.4 implies that \mathrm{TD}(\rho^{x},\texttt{CZ}_{m}\cdot\rho^{x}\cdot\texttt{CZ}_{m})\leq 2\sqrt{\varepsilon_{x}}.
Lemma 5.4.
Let \rho be a quantum mixed state on m qubits, and let \delta=\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}.
Then,
\displaystyle\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\texttt{CZ}_{m}\cdot\rho\cdot\texttt{CZ}_{m})\leq 2\sqrt{\delta}.
(70)
Therefore, removing the CZ gate, barely changes the circuit functionality. More formally, denote by C^{\prime\prime\prime} the circuit C^{\prime\prime} with gate g replaced with identity.
Then,
\displaystyle\|f_{C^{\prime\prime}}-f_{C^{\prime\prime\prime}}\|_{2}^{2}
\displaystyle=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[(f_{C^{\prime\prime}}(x)-f_{C^{\prime\prime\prime}}(x))^{2}]
(71)
\displaystyle\leq\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}\left[\mathrm{TD}(\rho^{x},\texttt{CZ}_{m}\cdot\rho^{x}\cdot\texttt{CZ}_{m})^{2}\right]
(72)
\displaystyle\leq\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[\varepsilon_{x}]
(73)
\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon/8.
(74)
The circuit C^{\prime\prime\prime} (without gate g replaced with identity) has only one layer of CZ gates, and its output depends on only a single input qubit, i.e., it computes a dictator function. Such a circuit has zero Fourier weight above level 1, let alone k. Thus, via Lemma 5.5, our circuit C^{\prime\prime} has at most \varepsilon/4 Fourier weight above level k.
Lemma 5.5.
[Closeness in \ell_{2} implies closeness in Fourier tails]
Let f,g:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}}, with \|f\|_{2},\|g\|_{2}\leq 1 and let k\in{\mathbb{N}}. Then, |{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f]-{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[g]|\leq 2\cdot\|f-g\|_{2}^{2}
Case 2: g is active with non-neglible probability.
Otherwise, \bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}\geq\varepsilon/8. Using the fact that \rho=\rho_{0}\otimes\rho_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes\rho_{n},
\displaystyle\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}=\prod_{i=0}^{n}\bra{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\rho_{i}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\geq\varepsilon/32\;.
(75)
Denoting \delta_{i}=1-\bra{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\rho_{i}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}}, this implies that
\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n}\delta_{i}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\left(1-\bra{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\rho_{i}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\right)\leq\sum_{i=0}^{n}1/\ln(1/\bra{1^{|Q_i|}}\rho_i \ket{1^{|Q_i|}})\rho_{i}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\leq\ln(32/\eps).
(76)
Therefore, for most i\in[n], \bra{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\rho_{i}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}} is rather close to 1.
Also note that both
\displaystyle\bra{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\rho_{i}^{0}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\geq 1-2\delta_{i}\quad\text{ and }\quad\bra{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\rho_{i}^{1}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\geq 1-2\delta_{i},
(77)
so Lemma 5.6 implies that \mathrm{TD}(\rho_{i}^{0},\rho_{i}^{1})\leq 8\sqrt{\delta_{i}}.
Lemma 5.6.
Let 0\leq\delta\leq 1.
Suppose \rho^{\prime} and \rho^{\prime\prime} are two mixed states on d qubits, such that \bra{1^{d}}\rho^{\prime}\ket{1^{d}}\geq 1-\delta and \bra{1^{d}}\rho^{\prime\prime}\ket{1^{d}}\geq 1-\delta.
Then, \mathrm{TD}(\rho^{\prime},\rho^{\prime\prime})\leq 2\delta+2\sqrt{\delta}.
Next, we prove a Fourier tail bound for this case.
We observe that
\rho_{i}^{x_{i}}=\rho_{i}+(-1)^{x_{i}}\cdot D_{i}\qquad\text{where}\qquad D_{i}=\frac{\rho_{i}^{1}-\rho_{i}^{0}}{2}
is the derivative of \rho_{i}^{x_{i}} according to x_{i}.
This will allow us to write a nice “matrix Fourier decomposition” for \rho and a bound on the Fourier spectrum of f_{C^{\prime\prime}}.
With this notation,
\displaystyle\rho
\displaystyle=\rho_{0}\otimes\bigg(\rho_{1}+(-1)^{x_{1}}\cdot D_{1}\bigg)\otimes\dots\otimes\bigg(\rho_{n}+(-1)^{x_{n}}\cdot D_{n}\bigg)
\displaystyle=\sum_{R\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{\sum_{i\in R}x_{i}}\cdot\rho_{0}\otimes\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}[(\rho_{i})^{{\mathbbm{1}}_{i\not\in R}}(D_{i})^{{\mathbbm{1}}_{i\in R}}]
So, we can think of the coefficient of (-1)^{\sum_{i\in R}x_{i}} as the R-Fourier coefficient of \rho.
That is,
\widehat{\rho}(R):=\rho_{0}\otimes\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}[(\rho_{i})^{{\mathbbm{1}}_{i\not\in R}}(D_{i})^{{\mathbbm{1}}_{i\in R}}].
Note that the R-Fourier coefficient in this case is a matrix (instead of a scalar in the standard case).
Since all density matrices have trace-norm 1, \|\rho_{i}\|_{1}=1 for all i\in[n]. Therefore, since the trace is multiplicative with respect to tensor products,
\displaystyle\|\widehat{\rho}(R)\|_{1}=\prod_{i\in R}\|D_{i}\|_{1}.
(78)
Furthermore, observe that, by definition of trace distance, \|D_{i}\|_{1}=\mathrm{TD}(\rho_{i}^{1},\rho_{i}^{0}) .
Now, f_{C^{\prime\prime}}(x) is an application of a unitary U and a projection \Pi on \rho^{x}. As such,
\displaystyle f_{C^{\prime\prime}}(x)=\Tr(\Pi U \rho^x U^{\dagger} )
\displaystyle=\Tr\left(\Pi U\sum_{R\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{\sum_{i\in R}x_{i}}\widehat{\rho}(R)U^{\dagger}\right)=\sum_{R\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{\sum_{i\in R}x_{i}}\Tr(\Pi U \widehat{\rho}(R) U^{\dagger} ).
From hereon, we will denote \widehat{f_{C^{\prime\prime}}}(R)=\Tr(\Pi U \widehat{\rho}(R) U^{\dagger}). By properties of the trace norm, |\widehat{f_{C^{\prime\prime}}}(R)|\leq\|\widehat{\rho}(R)\|_{1}. Thus, by Equation 78,
\displaystyle|\widehat{f_{C^{\prime\prime}}}(R)|\leq\|\widehat{\rho}(R)\|_{1}=\prod_{i\in R}\|D_{i}\|_{1}=\prod_{i\in R}\mathrm{TD}(\rho_{i}^{0},\rho_{i}^{1})\leq\prod_{i\in R}8\sqrt{\delta_{i}}.
(79)
Therefore, for any \ell\in{\mathbb{N}},
\displaystyle{\mathsf{W}}^{\ell}[f_{C^{\prime\prime}}]=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}R\subseteq[n]:\\
|R|=\ell\end{subarray}}|\widehat{f}_{C^{\prime\prime}}(R)|^{2}
\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}R\subseteq[n]:\\
|R|=\ell\end{subarray}}~\prod_{i\in R}(64\delta_{i})
\displaystyle\leq\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(64\delta_{i}))^{\ell}}{\ell!}
(Maclaurin’s Inequality)
\displaystyle\leq\frac{(64\ln(32/\eps))^{\ell}}{\ell!}\leq\left(\frac{e\cdot 64\ln(32/\eps)}{\ell}\right)^{\ell}\;.
To obtain {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C^{\prime\prime}}]\leq\varepsilon/4, it suffices to pick k=2e\cdot 64\ln(32/\eps)=\Theta(\ln(1/\eps)).
∎
5.2 Influence and Parity Correlation Bounds
Before proving the lemmata and claims used in the proof of Theorem 5.1, we prove three useful corollaries on the Fourier tails of f_{C}: (i) a bound on the tail {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}] for k in terms of k and n, (ii) a bound on the total influence of f_{C}, and (iii) a bound on the correlation of f_{C} with the PARITY function.
All follow easily from Theorem 5.1.
Corollary 5.7.
Let c>1 be the constant in Theorem 5.1.
For level k\leq 2c\log^{2}n, we have {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\exp(-\Omega(k/\log n)), and
for level k\geq 2c\log^{2}n, we have
{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\exp(-\Omega(\sqrt{k})).
Proof.
Theorem 5.1 implies that for any s\geq 0, if we want to get a Fourier tail bound of {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f]\leq 2^{-s} it suffices to take k=c\log(1/2^{-s})\log(n/2^{-s})=cs(s+\log n).
We consider two cases separately depending on whether s\leq\log n or not.
Note that s\leq\log n if and only if k\leq 2c\log^{2}n, so we divide to cases based on this condition.
The Case k\leq 2c\log^{2}n.
Let s=k/(2c\log n)\leq\log n and take \varepsilon=2^{-s}.
We want to show that {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon.
Indeed, we know that {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq\kappa(\varepsilon)}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon
for
\kappa(\varepsilon)=c\log(1/\eps)(\log(n/\eps))=cs(\log n+s)\leq 2cs\log n\leq k.
By monotonicity of Fourier tails we get
{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq W^{\geq\kappa(\varepsilon)}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon=2^{-k/2c\log n}.
The Case k\geq 2c\log^{2}n.
Let s=\sqrt{k/2c}\geq\log n and take \varepsilon=2^{-s}.
We want to show that {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon.
Indeed, we know that {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq\kappa(\varepsilon)}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon for \kappa(\varepsilon)=cs(\log n+s)\leq 2cs^{2}\leq k.
Thus, we get {\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq W^{\geq\kappa(\varepsilon)}[f_{C}]\leq 2^{-\sqrt{k/2c}}
∎
Corollary 5.8.
{\mathbf{Inf}}[f_{C}]\leq O(\log n).
Proof.
By the definition of total influence,
\displaystyle{\mathbf{Inf}}[f_{C}]=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}|S|\cdot\widehat{f}_{C}(S)^{2}=\sum_{k>1}k\cdot{\mathsf{W}}^{=k}[f_{C}]=\sum_{k>1}{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}].
(80)
Corollary 5.7 shows that
\displaystyle{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\begin{cases}\exp(-\Omega(k/\log n)),&\text{if }k\leq 2c\log^{2}n\\
\exp(-\Omega(\sqrt{k})),&\text{if }k\geq 2c\log^{2}n\end{cases}.
(81)
Thus, for some constants \alpha and \beta, the total influence can be bounded as
\displaystyle{\mathbf{Inf}}[f_{C}]\leq\sum_{k\leq 2c\log^{2}n}\exp(-\alpha k/\log n)+\sum_{k>2c\log^{2}n}\exp(-\beta\sqrt{k})=O(\log n).
∎
Corollary 5.9.
f_{C} is weakly correlated with PARITY, i.e. \langle f_{C},\chi_{[n]}\rangle\leq\exp(-\Omega(\sqrt{n})).
Proof.
The correlation of f_{C} with the PARITY function \chi_{[n]} is
\displaystyle\langle f_{C},\chi_{[n]}\rangle=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat{f}_{C}(S)\cdot\widehat{\chi}_{[n]}(S)=\widehat{f}_{C}([n])=\sqrt{{\mathsf{W}}^{=n}[f_{C}]}.
(82)
Via Corollary 5.7, {\mathsf{W}}^{=n}[f_{C}]\leq\exp\left(-\Omega(\sqrt{n})\right) for n large enough (as it satisfies n\geq 2c\log^{2}n), which implies the desired result.
∎
subsectionProofs of Claims and Lemmata
We now provide the proofs of the intermediate claims and lemmas used in the proof of Theorem 5.1.
See 5.5
Proof of Lemma 5.5.
\displaystyle\left|{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f]-{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[g]\right|
\displaystyle=\left|\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x}[f^{\geq k}(x)^{2}-g^{\geq k}(x)^{2}]\right|
\displaystyle=\left|\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x}[(f^{\geq k}(x)-g^{\geq k}(x))\cdot(f^{\geq k}(x)+g^{\geq k}(x))]\right|
\displaystyle\leq\|f^{\geq k}-g^{\geq k}\|_{2}\cdot\|f^{\geq k}+g^{\geq k}\|_{2}
(Cauchy-Schwarz)
\displaystyle\leq\|f^{\geq k}-g^{\geq k}\|_{2}\cdot(\|f^{\geq k}\|_{2}+|g^{\geq k}\|_{2})
(Triangle Inequality)
\displaystyle\leq\|f-g\|_{2}\cdot(\|f\|_{2}+|g\|_{2})
\displaystyle\leq 2\cdot\|f-g\|_{2}.\qed
We call a random restriction, (J,z), “random valued” if J\subseteq[n] is picked under some arbitrary distribution but given J, z is sampled uniformly at random from {\{0,1\}}^{[n]\setminus J}.
See 5.2
Proof of Claim 5.2.
Denote by m the number of qubits on which the CZ gate g depends on.
Let \ket{\psi^{x_{S}}_{g}} be the pure state entering the gate g, as a function of x_{S}. Let \ket{\psi^{x_{\overline{S}}}_{rest}} be the rest of the state as a function of x_{\overline{S}}. So, for any x\in{\{0,1\}}^{n} we have that the state entering the layer 1 gates is
\ket{\psi^{x}}=\ket{\psi^{x_{S}}_{g}}\otimes\ket{\psi^{x_{\overline{S}}}_{rest}}.
Removing the CZ gate is the same as considering the behavior of the circuit on the state
\texttt{CZ}_{m}\ket{\psi^{x}}=(\texttt{CZ}_{m}\ket{\psi^{x_{S}}_{g}})\otimes\ket{\psi^{x_{\overline{S}}}_{rest}}\;.
So to show that the function f_{C} associated with the original circuit C and the function f_{C^{\prime}} associated with the circuit C^{\prime}, where g is replaced with identity, are close in \ell_{2}-distance it suffices to show that the states are \texttt{CZ}_{m}\ket{\psi^{x}} and \ket{\psi^{x}} are close for most x.
\displaystyle\|f_{C}-f_{C^{\prime}}\|_{2}^{2}
\displaystyle=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[(f_{C}(x)-f_{C^{\prime}}(x))^{2}]
\displaystyle\leq\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[\mathrm{TD}(\ket{\psi^{x}},\texttt{CZ}_{m}\ket{\psi^{x}})^{2}]
\displaystyle=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[\mathrm{TD}(\ket{\psi_{g}^{x_{S}}},\texttt{CZ}_{m}\ket{\psi_{g}^{x_{S}}})^{2}]
\displaystyle=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[1-|\braket{\psi_{g}^{x_{S}}|\texttt{CZ}_{m}|\psi_{g}^{x_{S}}}|^{2}]
\displaystyle=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[1-(1-2|\braket{\psi_{g}^{x_{S}}|0^{m}}|^{2})^{2}]
\displaystyle=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[4|\braket{\psi_{g}^{x_{S}}|0^{m}}|^{2}-4|\braket{\psi_{g}^{x_{S}}|0^{m}}|^{4}]
\displaystyle\leq 4\cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[|\braket{\psi_{g}^{x_{S}}|0^{m}}|^{2}]
Since \ket{\psi_{g}^{x_{S}}} is separable we can write it as \ket{\psi_{g}^{x_{s}}}=\ket{\psi_{g}^{(0)}}\otimes\bigotimes_{i\in S}\ket{\psi_{i}^{x_{i}}} so that
\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[|\braket{\psi_{g}^{x_{S}}|0^{m}}|^{2}]=|\braket{\psi_{g}^{0}|\vec{0}}|^{2}\cdot\prod_{i\in S}\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x}[|\braket{\psi_{i}^{x_{i}}|0}|^{2}]
To finish the proof, we claim that for any i\in S, \mathop{\bf E\/}_{x}[\braket{\psi_{i}^{x_{i}}|0}|^{2}]=1/2.
Indeed, this is the average of |\braket{\psi_{i}^{0}|0}|^{2} and |\braket{\psi_{i}^{1}|0}|^{2}, and the vectors \ket{\psi_{i}^{0}},\ket{\psi_{i}^{1}} form an orthogonal basis over {\mathbb{C}}^{2}, so the average inner product squared with any fixed vector will be 1/2.
The claim about Fourier tails follows from
Lemma 5.5.
∎
See 5.3
Proof of Claim 5.3.
By the behavior of Fourier weight under random-valued restrictions, i.e., by Lemma 3.2, we have
\displaystyle\mathop{\bf E\/}_{J,z}[{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f|_{J,z}]]
\displaystyle=\sum_{R\subseteq[n]}\widehat{f}(R)^{2}\cdot\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[|R\cap J|\geq k]\geq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}R\subseteq[n]:\\
|R|\geq 4kb\end{subarray}}\widehat{f}(R)^{2}\cdot\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[|R\cap J|\geq k]
Thus, it suffices to prove that for any set R of size at least 4kb, the probability \mathop{\bf Pr\/}[|R\cap J|\geq k]\geq 1/2.
Partition R according to the blocks S_{0},S_{1},\ldots,S_{\ell}, by taking R_{0}=R\cap S_{0},\ldots,R_{\ell}=R\cap S_{\ell}. For each i\in\{0,1,\ldots,\ell\} the probability that |R_{i}\cap J|=1 is at least |R_{i}|/b, and these events are independent. In expectation we have \mathop{\bf E\/}[\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}|R_{i}\cap J|]=\mathop{\bf E\/}[|R\cap J|]\geq\frac{|R|}{b}\geq 4k. By Chernoff bound, we get that the probability that \sum_{i=1}^{\ell}|R_{i}\cap J|\geq k is at least 1-\exp(-(4k\cdot(3/4)^2)/2))\geq 1-\exp(-k)\geq 1/2 as required to finish the proof.
∎
We move on to prove Lemma 5.4. Before doing so, we will need the following additional lemma.
Lemma 5.10.
Let \rho be a quantum mixed state on finite domain X.
Then for each i\in X, \bra{i}\rho\ket{i}\geq\bra{i}\rho^{2}\ket{i}.
Proof of Lemma 5.10.
We will denote the eigenvectors of \rho as \{\ket{\psi_{j}}\}_{j\in X}, with corresponding eigenvalue \{\lambda_{j}\}_{j\in X} satisfying \lambda_{j}\in[0,1]. We can decompose the standard basis vectors in terms of these eigenvalues as
\displaystyle\ket{i}=\sum_{j\in X}\braket{\psi_{j}|i}\cdot\ket{\psi_{j}}=\sum_{j\in X}\alpha_{i,j}\cdot\ket{\psi_{j}},
(83)
which we can use to decompose \bra{i}\rho\ket{i} as
\displaystyle\bra{i}\rho\ket{i}
\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{k\in X}\alpha_{i,k}^{*}\cdot\bra{\psi_{k}}\right)\rho\left(\sum_{j\in X}\alpha_{i,j}\cdot\ket{\psi_{j}}\right)=\sum_{k,j\in X}\alpha_{i,k}^{*}\alpha_{i,j}\bra{\psi_{k}}\rho\ket{\psi_{j}}
(84)
\displaystyle=\sum_{k,j\in X}\alpha_{i,k}^{*}\alpha_{i,j}\lambda_{j}\braket{\psi_{k}|\psi_{j}}=\sum_{j\in X}|\alpha_{i,j}|^{2}\lambda_{j}.
(85)
We do the same for \rho^{2} which has the same eigenvectors as \rho, but eigenvalues \{\lambda_{j}^{2}\}_{j\in X} to get
\displaystyle\bra{i}\rho^{2}\ket{i}=\sum_{j\in X}|\alpha_{i,j}|^{2}\lambda_{j}^{2}.
(86)
Overall, this establishes that
\bra{i}\rho\ket{i}=\sum_{j\in X}|\alpha_{i,j}|^{2}\lambda_{j}\geq\sum_{j\in X}|\alpha_{i,j}|^{2}\lambda_{j}^{2}=\bra{i}\rho^{2}\ket{i}.\qed
With this, we can now prove Lemma 5.4.
See 5.4
Proof of Lemma 5.4.
Let \rho^{\prime}=\texttt{CZ}_{m}\cdot\rho\cdot\texttt{CZ}_{m}.
Then \bra{i}\rho^{\prime}\ket{j}=\bra{i}\rho\ket{j} if both i,j\neq 1^{m} or both are equal to 1^{m}, and \bra{i}\rho^{\prime}\ket{j}=-\bra{i}\rho\ket{j} otherwise.
We get that \mathrm{TD}(\rho,\texttt{CZ}_{m}\cdot\rho\cdot\texttt{CZ}_{m})=\frac{1}{2}\|A\|_{1} where A=\rho-\rho^{\prime} and \|A\|_{1} is the trace norm of A.
Observe that A is non-zero only on the last row and the last column, and that it diagonal is all zeros. Thus, it is a Hermitian matrix with rank 2 and trace 0 that has two real non-zero eigenvalues that sum up to 0, which we denote by \lambda and -\lambda.
Looking at A^{\dagger}A=A^{2} we see that it is a block matrix composed of a (2^{m}-1)\times(2^{m}-1) block and a 1\times 1 block. The entry in the 1\times 1 block is one of the eigenvalues of A^{2}, so it equals \lambda^{2} and also (by definition) equals \sum_{i\in\{0,1\}^{m}}|\bra{1^{m}}A\ket{i}|^{2}.
As the trace norm of A is 2|\lambda| we get
\displaystyle\|A\|_{1}=2|\lambda|=2\cdot\sqrt{\sum_{\{0,1\}^{m}\setminus\{1^{m}\}}|\bra{1^{m}}A\ket{i}|^{2}}
\displaystyle=2\cdot\sqrt{\sum_{i\in\{0,1\}^{m}\setminus\{1^{m}\}}|\bra{1^{m}}(2\rho)\ket{i}|^{2}}
\displaystyle\leq 4\cdot\sqrt{\sum_{i\in\{0,1\}^{m}}|\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{i}|^{2}}
\displaystyle=4\cdot\sqrt{|\bra{1^{m}}\rho^{2}\ket{1^{m}}|^{2}}
\displaystyle\leq 4\cdot\sqrt{\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}}
(Lemma 5.10)
\displaystyle=4\sqrt{\delta}.
∎
Next, we recall Lemma 5.6 and prove it.
See 5.6
Proof of Lemma 5.6.
We can assume \delta<1/3 without loss of generality, as \mathrm{TD}(\rho^{\prime},\rho^{\prime\prime})\leq 1\leq 2\delta+2\sqrt{\delta} otherwise.
By the triangle inequality (and symmetry), we have that
\displaystyle\mathrm{TD}(\rho^{\prime},\rho^{\prime\prime})\leq\mathrm{TD}(\rho^{\prime},\outerproduct*{1^d}{1^d})+\mathrm{TD}(\outerproduct*{1^d}{1^d},\rho^{\prime\prime})=\mathrm{TD}(\rho^{\prime},\outerproduct*{1^d}{1^d})+\mathrm{TD}(\rho^{\prime\prime},\outerproduct*{1^d}{1^d}).
(87)
Therefore, it suffices to show that \bra{1^{d}}\rho\ket{1^{d}}\geq 1-\delta implies \mathrm{TD}(\rho,\outerproduct*{1^d}{1^d})\leq\delta+\sqrt{\delta}, for any mixed state \rho.
Let \rho=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\outerproduct{\psi_i}{\psi_i}, where \sum_{i}\lambda_{i}=1.
We express \ket{1^{d}}=\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}\ket{\psi_{j}} as a linear combination of the eigenvectors of \rho^{\prime}.
Then, as in Equation 84,
1-\delta\leq\bra{1^{d}}\rho\ket{1^{d}}=\sum_{j}|\alpha_{j}|^{2}\lambda_{j}\leq\max_{j}|\alpha_{j}|^{2}\cdot\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}=\max_{j}|\alpha_{j}|^{2},
so there exists a j with |\alpha_{j}|^{2}\geq 1-\delta, and since \delta<1/3, j is unique.
This means that
|\braket{\psi_{j}|1^{d}}|^{2}=|\alpha_{j}|^{2}\geq 1-\delta.
Similarly,
1-\delta\leq\bra{1^{d}}\rho\ket{1^{d}}=\sum_{k}|\alpha_{k}|^{2}\lambda_{j}k\leq\max_{k}\lambda_{k}\cdot\sum_{k}|\alpha_{k}|^{2}=\max_{k}\lambda_{k}\;,
so there exists a k with \lambda_{k}\geq 1-\delta, and
since \delta<1/3, k is unique.
Furthermore, we will now show that it must be the case that
\displaystyle j={\arg\max}_{i}|\alpha_{i}|^{2}={\arg\max}_{i}\lambda_{i}=k,
(88)
which implies that there is a unique j such that
\displaystyle 1-\delta\leq|\alpha_{j}|^{2}\quad\text{and}\quad 1-\delta\leq\lambda_{j}.
We will prove this by contradiction. For contradiction, assume that Equation 88 is false so the above j and k are different.
Since \sum_{i}\lambda_{i}=1 and \lambda_{k}\geq 1-\delta we get that \lambda_{j}\leq\delta.
Using the assumption \delta\leq 1/3 this implies that
\bra{1^{d}}\rho\ket{1^{d}}=\sum_{i}|\alpha_{i}|^{2}\lambda_{i}\leq|\alpha_{j}|^{2}\cdot\delta+\sum_{i:i\neq j}|\alpha_{i}|^{2}=\left(\sum_{i}|\alpha_{i}|^{2}\right)-(1-\delta)|\alpha_{j}|^{2}\leq 1-(1-\delta)^{2}\leq 5/9.
However, this contradicts the assumption that \bra{1^{d}}\rho\ket{1^{d}}\geq 1-\delta>2/3.
Overall, we have shown that there exists an eigenvector of \rho, denoted \ket{\psi_{j}}, such that, by the definition of trace distance for pure states,
\displaystyle\mathrm{TD}(\outerproduct*{\psi_j}{\psi_j},\outerproduct*{1^d}{1^d})=\sqrt{1-|\braket{\psi_{j}|1^{d}}|^{2}}\leq\sqrt{1-(1-\delta)}=\sqrt{\delta}
(89)
and, since the trace norm can be expressed as the sum of the absolute values of the eigenvalues,
\displaystyle\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\outerproduct*{\psi_j}{\psi_j})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(|1-\lambda_{j}|+\sum_{k\neq j}|\lambda_{k}|\right)\leq\frac{1}{2}\cdot(\delta+\delta)=\delta
(90)
By triangle inequality, this therefore implies that \mathrm{TD}(\rho,\outerproduct*{1^d}{1^d})\leq\delta+\sqrt{\delta}. ∎
6 Depth-2 Circuits Cannot Construct a Nekomata
We will now prove that a depth-2 QAC0 circuit cannot exactly synthesize a generalized n-nekomata even with unlimited ancillae. We will refer to the definitions in Section 3.5.
The outline of our proof is as follows. Given a depth-d circuit that output a n-qubit nekomata, we will construct a separable state on some subset of qubits, \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q}, such that, inside the eigenspace of \outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}, (1) the state is still a nekomata and (2) the final layer is simplified to a single-qubit layer. The main idea behind this is the same as the block diagonalization used in Lemma 4.5. To complete our proof for d=2, we show that a depth-1 QAC circuit cannot compute a state that looks like an \Omega(1)-qubit nekomata, even after post-selecting for such \outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q} as in Definition 3.7
Then, the two main components are given by the following lemmas.
{restatable*}[Nekomata after one layer]lemmanekotognsp
Let \ket{\psi} be a n-nekomata. Then, for any layer L of separable reflection gates, the state \ket{\varphi} given by \ket{\varphi}=L\cdot\ket{\psi} is an \lceil n/2\rceil-GNSP.
{restatable*}
[No GNSP in depth-1]lemmaonelayergnsp
Let \ket{\psi} be a state constructed by a depth-1 QAC0 circuit C. Then, \ket{\psi} cannot be a n-GNSP for any n>2.
Then, the bound from Theorem 1.5 immediately follows as a consequence,
Corollary 6.1.
Let \ket{\psi} be a state constructed by a depth-2 QAC0 circuit C starting from the \ket{{\vec{0}}} state. Then, \ket{\psi} cannot be a generalized n-nekomata for n>4.
Proof.
Assuming for contradiction that \ket{\psi} is a generalized n-nekomata for n\geq 5. Then, letting \ket{\varphi} be the state after the first layer of C, \ket{\psi} is given by \ket{\psi}=L\cdot\ket{\varphi} for the second layer L.
Since all reflection gates are Hermitian, \ket{\varphi}=L\cdot\ket{\psi} and due to Section 6, \ket{\varphi} is an 3-GNSP. This is a contradiction to Section 6.
∎
6.1 Proofs of Lemmata
First, we show the following observation.
Fact 6.2.
Let \ket{\psi}_{T,A} be a generalized n-nekomata on targets t_{1},t_{2}\dots t_{n} and ancillae A. Then, for any unitary U_{A} acting only on the ancillae, the state U_{A}\cdot\ket{\psi} is still a generalized n-nekomata on targets t_{1},t_{2}\dots t_{n}.
Proof.
Suppose \ket{\psi} is given by,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi}
\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\ket{\mu_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}
(91)
Then,
\displaystyle U_{A}\cdot\ket{\psi}
\displaystyle=\alpha\ket{\mu_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu_{n}}_{t_{n}}U_{A}\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}+\beta\ket{\mu_{1}^{\perp}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu_{2}^{\perp}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu_{n}^{\perp}}_{t_{n}}U_{A}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}
(92)
which is also a generalized n-nekomata on the same targets.
∎
Now we provide the proofs of the lemmas. First, we will prove a special case of Section 6 for a single gate.
Claim 6.3.
Let \ket{\psi} be a generalized n-nekomata on targets T and \ket{\varphi}=G(S)\cdot\ket{\psi}, where G(S)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}) is a reflection gate on a subset of qubits S containing k=\left\lvert S\cap T\right\rvert targets.
Then, there exists a separable state \ket{\eta}_{Q} on qubits Q\subseteq S, such that, \outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\varphi} is a generalized n-\lfloor k/2\rfloor-nekomata.
Proof.
Wlog \ket{\psi} is given by,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi}
\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\ket{0^{n}}_{T}\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\ket{1^{n}}_{T}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}
(93)
For every qubit q\in S, let \ket{\theta^{\perp}_{q}} be such that \braket{\theta_{q}|\theta^{\perp}_{q}}=0, then, wlog \bra{\theta^{\perp}_{q}}\cdot\ket{\psi}\neq 0, otherwise q is redundant in G(S) and we can remove it to get a smaller gate. If S\cap T=\emptyset, then \ket{\varphi} is already a generalized n-nekomata due to Fact 6.2. Otherwise we have two main cases.
At least two targets in gate, \left\lvert S\cap T\right\rvert\geq 2:
Suppose there is a target t\in T\cap S such that, 0<\left\lvert\braket{\theta_{t}|0}\right\rvert<1. Then, for \ket{\eta}=\ket{\theta^{\perp}_{t}} we have \braket{\theta^{\perp}|0}\neq 0 and \braket{\theta^{\perp}|1}\neq 0. Therefore, the following state is a generalized (n-1)-nekomata on T^{\prime}=T\setminus t,
\displaystyle\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{t}\cdot\ket{\varphi}
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{t}\cdot\ket{\psi}\qquad\text{(since $\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{t}G(S)=\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{t}\otimes I$)}
(94)
\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\braket{\eta|0}\cdot\ket{\eta}_{t}\ket{0^{n-1}}_{T^{\prime}}\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\braket{\eta|1}\cdot\ket{\eta}_{t}\ket{1^{n-1}}_{T^{\prime}}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}
(95)
If no such t exists, then, observe that for every target t\in T,
\displaystyle[\outerproduct*{0}{0}_{t},G(S)]=[\outerproduct*{1}{1}_{t},G(S)]=0
(96)
\displaystyle\Rightarrow[\outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}_{T},G(S)]=[\outerproduct*{1^n}{1^n}_{T},G(S)]=0
(97)
Then, from Section 2.3.1, for unitaries U,V acting only on the ancillae S\setminus T,
\displaystyle\outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}_{T}\cdot G(S)
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}\otimes U_{S\setminus T}
(98)
\displaystyle\outerproduct*{1^n}{1^n}_{T}\cdot G(S)
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{1^n}{1^n}\otimes V_{S\setminus T}
(99)
Hence, \ket{\varphi} is already a generalized n-nekomata because,
\displaystyle\ket{\varphi}
\displaystyle=G(S)\cdot\ket{\psi}
(100)
\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\ket{0^{n}}_{T}\otimes U_{S^{\prime}}\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\ket{1^{n}}_{T}\otimes V_{S^{\prime}}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}
(101)
One target in gate
Let t=T\cap S and, S^{\prime}=S\setminus t and T^{\prime}=T\setminus S.
Then, we will prove by induction on m=|S^{\prime}| that for some product state \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q}, \outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\varphi} is actually a generalized n-nekomata. In the case when m=0, G(S) acts as a single qubit unitary on t and \ket{\varphi} is already a generalized n-nekomata. Now for m>1, let q\in S^{\prime} be any ancilla. First, if \bra{\theta}\cdot\ket{\psi}=0, or \bra{\theta^{\perp}_{q}}\cdot\ket{\psi}=0, we can either replace the gate with I or a smaller gate with q a before and apply the inductive hypothesis on m-1.
Wlog assume \ket{\theta_{q}}=\ket{1}_{q}. Suppose that for some value b\in\{0,1\},
\bra{b}_{q}\cdot\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}\neq 0 and \bra{b}_{q}\cdot\ket{\gamma_{1}}\neq 0. Then,
let \ket{\psi^{\prime}}\propto\outerproduct*{b}{b}\cdot\ket{\psi} and \ket{\varphi^{\prime}}\propto\outerproduct*{b}{b}\cdot\ket{\varphi}. Observe that \ket{\psi^{\prime}} is a generalized n-nekomata because,
\displaystyle\outerproduct*{b}{b}_{q}\cdot\ket{\psi}
\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\ket{0^{n}}_{T}\left(\outerproduct*{b}{b}_{q}\cdot\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}\right)+\beta\cdot\ket{1^{n}}_{T}\left(\outerproduct*{b}{b}_{q}\cdot\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}\right)
(102)
Furthermore, from Section 2.3.1, if b=0, \ket{\varphi^{\prime}}=\ket{\psi^{\prime}} and is also a generalized n-nekomata and we are done. If b=1, \ket{\varphi^{\prime}}=G(S\setminus q)\ket{\psi^{\prime}} where G(S\setminus q)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S\setminus q}), and let \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q^{\prime}} be the state from the inductive hypothesis on \ket{\varphi^{\prime}} and \ket{\psi^{\prime}} such that \outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q^{\prime}}\cdot\ket{\varphi^{\prime}} is a generalized n-1-nekomata. Then, by definition,
\displaystyle\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q^{\prime}}\cdot\ket{\varphi^{\prime}}
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q^{\prime}}\otimes\outerproduct*{1}{1}_{q}\cdot\ket{\varphi}
(103)
and therefore, for \ket{\eta_{q}}_{q}=\ket{1}_{q}, \outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q^{\prime},q}\cdot\ket{\varphi} is a generalized n-nekomata.
∎
This allows us to easily extend to general version, Section 6.
\nekotognsp
Proof.
Let T be the set of targets in \ket{\psi} and Q_{0} be the set of qubits belonging to the gates in L and n_{0}=\left\lvert T\cap Q_{0}\right\rvert be the number of targets from T in these gates. We will proceed by induction on m, the number of gates in L and additionally argue that, (1) Q\subseteq Q_{0}, (2) \outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\varphi} is a generalized nekomata on at least n-\lfloor n_{0}/2\rfloor targets.
For m=1, this simply follows from Claim 6.3. For m>1, let G(S)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}) be a gate in L so that L=G(S)\otimes L_{1}, where L_{1} contains m-1 gates and let n_{1} be the number of targets from T in L_{1} and n_{2}=n_{0}-n_{1} be the number of targets in S.
Then, from the inductive hypothesis on \ket{\varphi_{1}}=L_{1}\cdot\ket{\psi}, there is a state \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q_{1}} only on qubits in L_{1} such that the state \ket{\psi_{1}}\propto\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q_{1}}\cdot\ket{\varphi_{1}} is a generalized n-\lfloor n_{1}/2\rfloor-nekomata.
Now for \ket{\varphi_{2}}=G(S)\cdot\ket{\psi_{1}}, from Claim 6.3, there is a state \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q_{2}} on Q_{2}\subseteq S such that \ket{\psi_{2}}\propto\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q_{2}}\cdot\ket{\varphi_{2}} is a generalized n^{\prime} nekomata for,
\displaystyle n^{\prime}
\displaystyle=n-\lfloor n_{1}/2\rfloor-\lfloor n_{2}/2\rfloor
(104)
\displaystyle\geq n-\lfloor n_{0}/2\rfloor
(105)
Then, for Q=Q_{1}\cup Q_{2}\subseteq Q_{0} and \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q}=\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q_{1}}\otimes\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q_{2}},
\displaystyle\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\varphi}
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{\veta_Q}{\veta_Q}\cdot\left(G(S)\otimes L_{1}\right)\cdot\ket{\psi}
(106)
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{\veta_{Q_2}}{\veta_{Q_2}}\cdot G(S)\cdot\left(\outerproduct*{\veta_{Q_1}}{\veta_{Q_1}}\cdot L_{1}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right)
(107)
\displaystyle\propto\outerproduct*{\veta_{Q_2}}{\veta_{Q_2}}\cdot G(S)\cdot\ket{\psi_{1}}
(108)
\displaystyle\propto\ket{\psi_{2}}
(109)
which is a generalized n^{\prime}-nekomata.
∎
Finally, we will prove the base case of the result for depth-1 restated below,
\onelayergnsp
Proof.
Note that \ket{\psi} is separable across S_{1},S_{2}\dots S_{m}, the subset of qubits belonging to each of the m gates of C. Furthermore, for any separable state \ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q}, \outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\psi} is also separable across S_{1},S_{2}\dots S_{m}. Therefore, it suffices to prove the lemma for when C consisting of a single gate. Then, \ket{\psi}=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth^1}{\vth^1}_{S})\cdot\ket{\vec{\theta}^{0}}_{S} for separable states \ket{\vec{\theta}^{0}},\ket{\vec{\theta}^{1}} such that 0<\left\lvert\braket{\theta^{1}_{q}|\theta^{0}_{q}}\right\rvert<1 for every q\in S.
Now suppose for contradiction that there exists \ket{\vec{\eta}} on Q\subseteq S, s.t \outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\psi}\propto\ket{\varphi}_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q} and \ket{\varphi} is a generalized n\geq 3-nekomata as below,
\displaystyle\ket{\varphi}=\alpha\cdot\ket{0^{n}}_{T}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}+\beta\ket{1^{n}}_{T}\ket{\gamma_{2}}_{A}
(110)
for some \alpha\neq 0 and \beta\neq 0 such that S^{\prime}=T\cup A.
For any target t\in T, since 0<\left\lvert\braket{\theta^{0}_{t}|\theta^{1}_{t}}\right\rvert<1 there must be some b\in\{0,1\} for which 0<\left\lvert\braket{\theta^{b}_{t}|0}\right\rvert<1. Let \ket{\varphi^{\prime}}\propto\outerproduct*{\mu}{\mu}_{t}\cdot\ket{\varphi} for \ket{\mu} such that \braket{\mu|\theta^{b}_{t}}=0. Then, \ket{\varphi^{\prime}} is a is a generalized n-1-nekomata because,
\displaystyle\ket{\varphi^{\prime}}
\displaystyle\propto\outerproduct*{\mu}{\mu}\cdot\ket{\varphi}
(111)
\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\braket{\mu|0}\cdot\ket{0^{n-1}}_{T\setminus t}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}\ket{\mu}_{t}+\beta\cdot\braket{\mu|1}\cdot\ket{1^{n-1}}_{T\setminus t}\ket{\gamma_{2}}_{A}\ket{\mu}_{t}.
(112)
However, observe that \ket{\psi}\in\mathrm{span}\{\ket{\vec{\theta}^{1}}_{S},\ket{\vec{\theta}^{0}}_{S}\} and thus \ket{\varphi}\in\mathrm{span}\{\ket{\vec{\theta}^{1}}_{S^{\prime}},\ket{\vec{\theta}^{0}}_{S^{\prime}}\}. Since \outerproduct*{\mu}{\mu}_{t}\otimes I is orthogonal to \ket{\vec{\theta}^{b}}, for b^{\prime}=b\oplus 1 and S^{\prime\prime}=S\setminus t, we have
\ket{\varphi^{\prime}}\in\mathrm{span}\{\ket{\vec{\theta}^{b^{\prime}}_{S^{\prime\prime}}}\otimes\ket{\mu}\}. This is a contradiction to n>2 because \ket{\varphi^{\prime}} is separable across all its qubits and cannot be a generalized 2-nekomata.
∎

Appendix A Approximate to Exact PARITY Deferred Proofs
First we will formally prove the form of [29] that we require.
See 2.3
Proof.
We can implement the transformation \ket{\bm{x}}\ket{0^{n}}\mapsto\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{x_{1}\oplus x_{2},x_{2}\oplus x_{3}\dots x_{n}\oplus x_{1}} in 2 layers of \mathtt{CNOT} gates [29]. Observe that \ket{x_{1}\oplus x_{2},\dots x_{n}\oplus x_{1}} has parity 0 regardless of \bm{x}. This allows us to synthesize the below superposition of even parity strings from \ket{0^{2n}} in QNC0.
\displaystyle\ket{\nu^{*}}
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\sum_{\bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\ket{\bm{x}}_{A}\ket{x_{1}\oplus x_{2},x_{2}\oplus x_{3}\dots x_{n}\oplus x_{1}}_{B}
(113)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n-1}}}\sum_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\oplus\bm{y}=0}\ket{\nu(\bm{y})}_{A}\otimes\ket{\bm{y}}_{B}
(114)
Note that \ket{\nu^{*}} is simply the “Poor Man’s Cat State” ([29]) due to the entangled A register. Uncomputing \ket{\nu(\bm{y})} would produce a \ket{{}_{n-1}} which is not possible in QNC0.
WLOG suppose that \gamma>0 so that the output register t of C measures to \texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}) with probability p=1/2+\gamma/2 on a random input (otherwise flip the output of C). We will describe a circuit C^{\prime} that, on any input \bm{x}, outputs \texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}) with probability at least p=1/2+\left\lvert\gamma\right\rvert/2.
On input \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, using 2n additional ancillae, construct \ket{\nu^{*}} and then apply a single layer of \mathtt{CNOT} gates from each input qubit to a corresponding qubit in B, to obtain,
\displaystyle\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{0^{2n}}\mapsto\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n-1}}}\sum_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\oplus\bm{y}=0}\ket{\bm{y}}\ket{\nu(\bm{y})}_{A}\otimes\ket{x_{1}\oplus y_{1},\dots x_{n}\oplus y_{n}}_{B}
(115)
Then, we can in feed the B registers as inputs to C instead. Observe that, measuring the B register produces a uniformly random string with the same PARITY as \bm{x}, therefore, the output of C^{\prime} measures to \texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}) with probability at least p.
∎
See 2.2
Proof.
The proof follows through a series of reductions described below.
1.
Apply Claim 2.3 to obtain a depth-d_{0}=d+O(1) circuit C_{0} with a_{0}=a+O(n) ancillae that correctly computes PARITY with probability 1/2+|\rho|/2 on every input \bm{x}.
2.
Using FAN-OUT and MAJORITY gates of size k=\Theta(1/\rho^{2})=\Theta(\log^{2\delta}n), repeat C_{0} in parallel k times and output the MAJORITY of the runs. This gives C_{1} that, on every \bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n} correctly outputs \texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}) correctly wp \geq 0.999. C_{1} can be implemented in depth-d_{1}=d+O(1) using a_{1}=a_{0}\cdot O(n^{O}(\delta)) ancillae from C_{0} due to [24, 12].
3.
Turn C_{1} into a n+1-output circuit C_{2} that preserves the input registers, by simply making a classical copy of each input coordinate x_{i} in a single layer at the start and then running C using on these qubits instead. This only increases the depth to d_{3}=d_{2}+1 and the number of ancillae to d_{3}=a_{3}+O(n).
4.
Apply the approximate reduction of [24] to obtain a depth-d_{4}=O(d) and a_{4}=O(a) circuit C_{4} such that the phase dependent fidelity of \ket{\psi}=C_{4}\cdot\ket{0^{n+a_{4}}} with \ket{{}_{n}}_{T} is at least 0.99. In other words, there is some ancilla state \ket{\alpha}_{A} such that,
1-\left\lVert\ket{\psi}_{T,A}-\ket{{}_{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha}_{A}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq 0.9.
Then, the qubits T of \ket{\psi} have at least 0.25 probability of measuring to all 0s and at least 0.25 probability of measuring to all 1s.
5.
Apply Claim 2.4 to obtain C_{5} for exactly computing \ket{{}_{n}} in depth-d_{5}=O(d_{4}) using a_{5}=a_{4}+1 ancillae.
This produces a depth-O(d) circuit with O(a\cdot n^{O(\delta)}) ancillae to exctly compute \ket{{}_{n}}. This can be turned into C^{\prime} for computing exact PARITY on n coordinates in depth-O(d) using a^{\prime}=O(d\cdot n^{O(\delta)}) ancillae [19].
The depth of C^{\prime} we obtain is independent in the original error and, when \rho=1/\text{poly}\log(n), C^{\prime} only requires a^{\prime}=\text{poly}(n) ancillae.
∎
See 2.4
Proof.
Let \alpha_{b}=\left\lvert\bra{b^{n}}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rvert for b\in\{0,1\}. Assume WLOG that \alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{0}. Using a fresh ancilla q, we will first apply a single gate G(T,q) on \ket{\psi}\otimes\ket{\mu}_{q} to produce a state \ket{\psi_{1}} with exactly 1/{2\sqrt{2}} amplitude on the two branches \ket{0^{n}}_{T}\ket{0}_{q} and \ket{1^{n}}_{T}\ket{0}_{q}. To achieve this, let \ket{\mu}=\beta\ket{0}+\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}\ket{1} for \beta=\frac{1}{\alpha_{0}2\sqrt{2}}
and choose G(T,q) to be a controlled-U_{q} gate, controlled on T being \ket{1^{n}}.
such that U maps \ket{0}\mapsto\gamma\ket{0}+\sqrt{1-\gamma^{2}}\ket{1} for \gamma=\frac{\alpha_{0}}{\alpha_{1}}. Note that we can set remaining degrees of freedom to make U=U^{\dagger} (valid reflection) as,
\displaystyle U:=\begin{bmatrix}\gamma&\sqrt{1-\gamma^{2}}\\
\sqrt{1-\gamma^{2}}&-\gamma\end{bmatrix}
(116)
This produces,
\displaystyle\left\lvert\bra{0^{n},0}_{T,q}\cdot\ket{\psi_{0}}\right\rvert
\displaystyle=\left\lvert\bra{0^{n}}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rvert\cdot\beta=\alpha_{0}\cdot\beta=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}
(117)
\displaystyle\left\lvert\bra{1^{n},0}_{T,q}\cdot\ket{\psi_{0}}\right\rvert
\displaystyle=\left\lvert\bra{1^{n}}\cdot\ket{\psi}\otimes U_{q}\ket{\mu}_{q}\right\rvert=\alpha_{1}\cdot\gamma\cdot\beta=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}
(118)
Define \Pi^{*}:=\left(\outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}_{T}+\outerproduct*{1^n}{1^n}_{T}\right)\otimes\outerproduct*{0}{0}_{q}
and let C_{0} be this depth-d+1 circuit to construct \ket{\psi_{0}} from \ket{0^{a+1}}, by applying a single qubit unitary \ket{0}_{q}\mapsto\ket{\mu}_{q} and then G(T,q)\cdot C. We claim that the following circuit synthesizes an n-nekomata,
\displaystyle C^{\prime}
\displaystyle:=(I-2\outerproduct*{\psi_0}{\psi_0})\cdot(I-2\Pi^{*})\cdot C_{0}
(119)
\displaystyle=C^{\dagger}_{0}(I-2\outerproduct*{0^{a+1}}{0^{a+1}})C_{0}\cdot(I-2\outerproduct*{0^n,0}{0^n,0}_{T,q})\cdot(I-2\outerproduct*{1^n,0}{1^n,0}_{T,q})\cdot C_{0},
(120)
Then, C^{\prime} only requires depth-d^{\prime}=3(d+1)+2\leq 3(d+2) and a+1 ancillae.
We now proceed to prove the remaining claim. Due to Equation 117 and Equation 118, there exists a n-nekomata \ket{\nu_{n}}_{T,A} such that,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{0}}
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\ket{\nu_{n}}\ket{0}_{q}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\ket{\varphi^{\prime}}
(121)
for some state \ket{\varphi^{\prime}} satisfying \Pi^{*}\cdot\ket{\varphi^{\prime}}=0. Since \ket{\nu_{n}}\ket{0}_{q}\in\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{*}),
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}}
\displaystyle:=(I-2\Pi^{*})\cdot C_{0}\ket{0^{a+1}}
(122)
\displaystyle=(I-2\Pi^{*})\cdot\ket{\psi_{0}}
(123)
\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot\ket{\nu_{n}}\ket{0}_{q}+\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{q}\cdot\ket{\varphi^{\prime}}
(124)
\displaystyle=\ket{\psi_{0}}-\ket{\nu_{n}}\ket{0}
(125)
Hence,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{2}}
\displaystyle:=C^{\prime}\ket{0^{a+1}}
(126)
\displaystyle=(I-2\outerproduct*{\psi_0}{\psi_0})\cdot\ket{\psi_{1}}
(127)
\displaystyle=\ket{\psi_{1}}-\ket{\psi_{0}}
(128)
\displaystyle=-\ket{\nu_{n}}\ket{0}
(129)
which is a n-qubit nekomata.
∎
